speechtext:
I do not intend to allow the hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Haggart) to misrepresent me in this matter. When, early in his speech, I called his attention to the fact that he was misrepresenting me, I thought he would make the amend and acknowledge that the language of mine that he quoted did not bear out the statement that he had made. The hon. gentleman attempted to bolster up his statement that I had always claimed that the Northern Light was an efficient boat, and in compliance with the terms of tile union, by reading what 1 had said. But it proved to be the very opposite of what he attributed to me. The statement that I made then, and that I make now, is that the Northern Light was a bona fide effort to carry out the terms of the union, and, so far as the spring and fall was concerned, the boat was efficient, but that for mid-winter she was entirely unsuccessful. I read to the House the other day from sta-

tistics furnished to the government in this matter, the number of days during which the Northern Light was unable to carry out this contract. The figures showed that, for two mouths, for two months and a half at a time, the Northern Light never crossed from one side to the other ; and the 120,000 people on the island were cut off from access to the mainland, because this inefficient boat was put on designed to carry out the contract that the Dominion had made.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

maintopic: P. E. I. CLAIMS-MAINTENANCE OF STEAM COMMUNICATION.
speechtext:
Did the hon. minister take any action to remedy the grievance at that time ?
The	MINISTER	OF	MARINE	AND
FISHERIES. I did not come to this House until 1882.

maintopic: P. E. I. CLAIMS-MAINTENANCE OF STEAM COMMUNICATION.
speechtext:
Mas that the year the question was brought up in this House ?
The	MINISTER	OF	MARINE	AND
FISHERIES. We had it up every year. Hon. members wTho were here in 1882 will remember

maintopic: P. E. I. CLAIMS-MAINTENANCE OF STEAM COMMUNICATION.
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman was supporting the	party	in power.The	MINISTER	OF	MARINE	AND
FISHERIES. I do not care what party was in power. The Liberal party was in power from 1873 to 1878, and from 1873 to 1876 there was no boat at all on the route except the old Albert, and she was confessedly a complete and absolute failure. For three years, the people had no communication at all by steam with the mainland, though the Dominion had contracted solemnly to give them continuous communication winter and summer. What does it matter which government failed to carry out that compact ?

maintopic: P. E. I. CLAIMS-MAINTENANCE OF STEAM COMMUNICATION.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman knows that continuous communication is not afforded even now.

maintopic: P. E. I. CLAIMS-MAINTENANCE OF STEAM COMMUNICATION.
speechtext:
There is no use quibbling about this matter. When I came into parliament there was a proposition brought forward by government supporters to build a submarine railway, which would cost from $5,000,000 to $8,000,000. I never gave my support to that project. I believed that there were means by which efficient steam communication could be maintained. It was a mere matter of using the proper means to that end, and in a short time these means were found. When the Stanley was put on in 1888, she was found efficient, and when this was supplemented by the Minto, it was proven that there was no difficulty in carrying out the compact that had been made. So, from the first, I have sounded one note- that the Dominion had failed to carry out its compact, that in that way it had done untold injury to the island, and that the island had a bona fide claim for recompense. And, now, I am proud to say, the Dominion Sir LOUIS DAVIES.
has recognized the claim. Not the whole, not even half of the claim made by the Conservative government of Prince Edward Island, and submitted to the Queen, which claim was for $5,000,000, but only one-fifth of it has been recognized. The hon. member (Hon. Mr. Haggart) says he is not going to quarrel with the amount. Then, what are we disputing about ? The fact that the compact has not been kept has been admitted. Surely, the claim to compensation is clear. Then, what are we taking up time for ? Are the rights of the province of Prince Edward Island to be ignored because it is a small province ? Shall this great Dominion stand before the world saying that it denies justice to one of its own provinces with which it has made a contract, which contract it has broken-that it will not pay honest damages? No honest man will take that position. The contract is so plain that no man can read it and have any doubt about what it means :
The Dominion government shall assume and defray all the charges for the following services, viz.: Efficient steam service for the conveyance of mails and passengers to be established and maintained between the island and the mainland of the Dominion winter and summer.
And, as if to place beyond the possibility of doubt what was meant by that-it went on-
Thus placing the Dominion in continuous communication with the Intercolonial Railway and the railway system of the Dominion.
It was on that agreement that the people of the island were induced to come into confederation. The people voted for confederation and put down those who were opposed to it, largely because of that promise, and that contract. And, having got the island into confederation, what did you do ? For three years you did not put a steamer on at all ; between 1876 and 1888 you made what, I admit, was a bona fide attempt to carry out the contract, but it was a complete failure ; in 1888 you did what you should have done from the first, built a first-class steel steamship ; and from that time you have substantially carried out the contract. And am I to be told that even though, for sixteen years the contract was not carried out and the people of the island were isolated the whole winter, suffering untold loss, yet, because they have no legal claim that they can enforce in the courts, their claim is to be repudiated. There may be differences of opinion as to the amount, though I have yet to hear any hon. gentleman say that the amount was not fair. This is one-fifth of what the province claims ; but they were willing to compromise owing to the length of time the matter had been pending, and to accept the compromise. And I think that every fair-minded man, looking at the circumstances all round, will say that this is a just and honest compromise. But to attempt to twist it into a change in the terms of the union is most un-

fair. This has nothing to do with additional subventions or a change in the terms of the union ; it is a fair settlement of an honest claim made by the province against the Dominion, a claim arising out of the failure of the Dominion to carry out its compact with the province, a claim that you cannot, in honesty, ignore.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

maintopic: P. E. I. CLAIMS-MAINTENANCE OF STEAM COMMUNICATION.
speechtext: The Prime Minister asked what we had to bring forward, and the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat was asked why we were taking up the time of the House. Well, at least we have got this far-it is proposed to give the province of Prince Edward Island $1,000,000. It is also brought out that it is proposed to vote this session $671,836 to the province of Nova Scotia. We are told this morning that another vote of a quarter of a million is to be made to the province of New Brunswick, and we are also told to-day that these two votes to the provinces of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia that will be proposed, are the result of an award going beyond the legal rights of the provinces.

maintopic: P. E. I. CLAIMS-MAINTENANCE OF STEAM COMMUNICATION.
speechtext: It would be better to discuss that matter when the votes come up on the resolution.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

maintopic: P. E. I. CLAIMS-MAINTENANCE OF STEAM COMMUNICATION.
speechtext: No, we are discussing the principle, and it is because there is no principle in this one, there is no submission to a proper court, that we are objecting. The Prime Minister laid it down a while ago that any question that should come up of this kind should be submitted to the courts to be settled, but he told us in connection with the claim of the settlers in the North-west with regard to the exemption of the Canadian Pacific Railway lands that equities were not to be considered. Now, that he has opened the door, what will be the nature of the settlement of these cleaims that will be coming after? It will be a reference of a claim on the principle of equity, and not of the legality of any claims that any province may put forward. After a good deal of discussion it has come out now that the door has been opened, that large subsidies are to be paid this session to the provinces, not on any legal claim, but as a matter of equity, as they call it, to the provinces. All the provinces will be filing similar claims, and I protest against any such thing being done with the money of the people.

maintopic: P. E. I. CLAIMS-MAINTENANCE OF STEAM COMMUNICATION.
speechtext:
My hon. friend had better wait until we bring forward these votes with regard to Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. If claims are pending against the Domininon, I lay it down as a principle for the guidance, of the party which is in power, whatever may be the policy of hon. gentlemen opposite, that these claims must be settled one way or the other. We shall not be afraid to take 16S
the responsibility of dealing in this parliament with any claim that can be presented by any province. I lay this down as a basis for the guidance of the government. upon which I invite the opposition to oppose us if they dare do so. With regard to the claim of New Brunswick, I may say to the hon. gentleman that if he had followed the history of this matter, he would know that this is not a new claim. It was dealt with a few years ago by the government of which he was a supporter, I think he was in the House at that time. The justice and fairness of that claim was acknowledged, but the interest upon it was not allowed ; and when the appropriation was brought before parliament at the time, a gentleman from New Brunswick supporting the government, Prof. Weldon, protested against the award being only for the principal and not for interest. He thought that if the province of New Brunswick was entitled to the money, it was entitled also to the interest upon it. We referred that matter to arbitration, and although the arbitrators were divided, the government made the appropriation, in order that New Brunswick should have no occasion to feel aggrieved. The same thing with reference to Nova Scotia. The hon. gentlemen are now raising their pi'otest in this matter after they had allowed the second reading to take place, and now when we are in committee simply to look after the terms of the Bill, they raise a discussion. If their arguments mean anything they should have been made against the second reading, but they did not dare to make their complaints at that time. What we want to know is whether they are for or against this Bill. If they are in favour of it, let them say so; if they are against it, let them have the courage of their opinions and vote against it. But for my part, I am not willing to allow hon. gentlemen to steer north by south and beat all about the bush; if they are against this Bill let them say so honestly and vote against it.

maintopic: P. E. I. CLAIMS-MAINTENANCE OF STEAM COMMUNICATION.
speechtext: Referring to a remark of the hon. member for Lanark (Hon. Mr. Haggart), who said there must be a finality to these things, almost in the same breath he said, no matter what you say in your statutes, there can be no finality, and no words you can put into the statute will make this matter final. I am rather disposed to accept that view. I venture to say that so long as we have a government or parliament ait -Ottawa, if any province makes a claim which seems to be fair and just, no matter what the past records may show, there will always be found a government and parliament willing to give it fair consideration, and if justice be

maintopic: P. E. I. CLAIMS-MAINTENANCE OF STEAM COMMUNICATION.
speechtext: I would hardly think if a province accepted a particular sum of money, a particular amount per annum from the government in satisfaction of a particular claim, and if it accepted it under the language of a statute declaring the settlement final, that it could reasonably make a claim with regard to that matter again unless it could show that there had been a clear mistake. Therefore, I would not concur in the view which the minister puts forward, that there can be no finality with regard to these things.

maintopic: P. E. I. CLAIMS-MAINTENANCE OF STEAM COMMUNICATION.
speechtext: Experience has shown it.

maintopic: P. E. I. CLAIMS-MAINTENANCE OF STEAM COMMUNICATION.
speechtext: I would not be prepared to concur in that view. If, however, the view which my hon. friend has put forward is correct, what becomes of the value of the assurance that he gave us a few moments ago, and which he was willing to have go down in the records, namely, that there is a distinct understanding in respect of alleged violations of the terms of confederation. If the statute is to be of no use in such a case, surely my hon. friend does not think his assurances given in this House when the Bill is in committee, will be of any service? I would hardly like to go that far. Now, in respect of what has been said by the right hon. leader of the government, I do not think that any criticism which has been made upon this Bill while in committee is at all out of place. The criticism has very properly been made that no basis has been pointed out upon which this amount has been fixed. I think we should have information in regard to that. Another thing which I would like to say to the* hon. Minister of Finance is, that if a claim in regard to the fisheries is to be disposed of at some time or other, why not dispose of it now in connection with this claim?

maintopic: P. E. I. CLAIMS-MAINTENANCE OF STEAM COMMUNICATION.
speechtext: It has not been settled by the court yet. The only decision that there would be a claim arising out of would be a decision that the provinces have territorial property in the three-mile limit. I do not agree with that contention. We take the very opposite ground. We say that the Dominion jurisdiction is absolute in regard to the fisheries and to navigation in the three-mile limit and that the provinces have no territorial rights. It is only if it is established that they have a territorial limit of three miles that they would have any claim under the fisheries award.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

maintopic: P. E. I. CLAIMS-MAINTENANCE OF STEAM COMMUNICATION.
speechtext:
Of course, if the hon. gentleman is correct in saying that something has to be determined by the

courts upon which the validity of such a claim depends, that is a sufficient reason for leaving that claim to he determined later. The hon. gentleman has not made it very clear to me what that question is. Not having examined very recently the decision of the Privy Council rendered some four years ago, I am perfectly clear yet as to what is left undetermined.

maintopic: P. E. I. CLAIMS-MAINTENANCE OF STEAM COMMUNICATION.
speechtext: There is a good deal left undetermined, hut there is this to be said about it, that what was determined was that so far as the rivers and inland lakes were concerned the property in those rivers and lakes was in the provinces, and that as a consequence the property in the fish pass to the provinces. Now, the question is : Does that also apply to the territorial waters in the sea? Some people say so, hut the Privy Council have not said so in so many words and we have tried to agree, and have agreed substantially upon a case, which would submit that very question to the courts. The decision is that the property in the rivers and lakes has remained with the provinces from confederation, and if so, would a similar result follow if the bed of the three-mile belt of the sea was judicially declared to be in the provinces ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

maintopic: P. E. I. CLAIMS-MAINTENANCE OF STEAM COMMUNICATION.
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I do not rise for the purpose of making any extended remarks on the subject of the Prince Edward Island matter, but more particularly to enter my protest against hon. gentlemen opposite introducing the subject of the New Brunswick claim as a matter germane to the present discussion. The effect of such introduction can only be to prejudice the minds of hon. gentlemen who hear what is said, and it can only do so in an unfair way because hon. members have not been put in possession of the facts which have led to the final settlement of the claim and they cannot possibly know the facts, even the hon. gentleman who leads in the condemnation of the claim. I would ask these hon. gentlemen what sort of an opinion anybody would form as to the weight or value of their judgment or as to the judicial manner in which they have approached the subject, when they have condemned the claim off-hand without knowing the facts ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

maintopic: P. E. I. CLAIMS-MAINTENANCE OF STEAM COMMUNICATION.
speechtext: May I ask the hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Blair) why members of the House have not been put in possession of the facts ?

maintopic: P. E. I. CLAIMS-MAINTENANCE OF STEAM COMMUNICATION.
speechtext:
I presume that if hon. gentlemen have asked me for information it has been furnished to them. If they have not asked for information, we are not to be held accountable. It must be admitted on all hands that the manner in which the government have dealt with the New Brunswick and Nova Scotia claims is not sufficient 1684
reason why the claim under consideration should be condemned. I take it that each one of these provinces is entitled to have these matters disposed of upon their individual merits, and that this case is not to be prejudiced because some one has an opinion on some other claim which another province has preferred. I take it that this is the spirit in which we would be expected to approach the consideration of this question. Now, if we are approaching the consideration of this question in that spirit the first thing that appears to me that we ought to ask ourselves is : What is the character of the compact that was entered into by the people of Canada with the province of Prince Edward Island on the strength of which the people of that province were induced to cast in their lot with us and become one of the provinces of federated Canada ? To ascertain what the nature of that pledge and compact was, it is material for us to consider it, not in a narrow and technical way as against the province, but in a broad spirit, not simply because the province is a little island which is cut off from the rest of Canada and which, by reason of its want of connection with the mainland, is denuded of many advantages which accrue to the remaining people of Canada by reason of the progress of public works and enterprise in which they are engaged. I do not put it in that way or on that ground, but the people of Prince Edward Island had the inducement held out to them, when they were urged to come into this confederation, that they might rely upon having the benefit of continuous connection with the Intercolonial Railway and with the mainland. That was the compact, and although my hon. friend (Hon. Sir Louis Davies) has already read it, I will read it again :
The Dominion government shall assume and defray all the charges for the following services, viz.: Efficient steam service for the conveyance of mails and passengers to be established and maintained between the island and the mainland of the Dominion winter and summer, thus placing the island in continuous communication with the Intercolonial Railway and the railway system of the Dominion.
Now, I want to know in what spirit the people of Canada should interpret that language when they know that that language was used in such a manner as to induce the people of Prince Edward Island to place confidence in it, to place their political interests in our hands and to enter into political connection with us. Ought we to take a view which is a narrow view, which is a lawyer's technical view, or ought we to view the matter in a broad spirit, and treat it as you would like it to be treated if you were the people of Prince Edward Island who had been induced to enter into confederation on the strength of the promises which were held out to them ? How does the hon. member for South Lanark propose to interpret the language of this

solemn compact and how does he say that this language ought to be interpreted ? I want to call the attention of the hon. gentleman to the language he has employed. He is not willing that that language shall be interpreted as a fair, square compact, made between the people of Canada and the people of Prince Edward Island. No, but he undertakes to change the language and to interpolate words into it so as to give a different meaning to it. He wants to say ' as far as possible,' or * as far as we possibly or reasonably can.' That is what he wants to say.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

maintopic: P. E. I. CLAIMS-MAINTENANCE OF STEAM COMMUNICATION.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: P. E. I. CLAIMS-MAINTENANCE OF STEAM COMMUNICATION.
speechtext: My hon. friend says 1 hear, hear.' He is not making a reasonable proposition when he asks to have the language changed in that way, and I will tell him why I do not think it is a reasonable proposition. It may be all very well if the hon. gentleman were interpreting the language of a contract between two individuals neither of whom was absolutely certain as to what he was doing, or sufficiently informed as to the nature of the contract that he was entering into. Will any one say that with such a knowledge of the facts as the government of Canada had at that time, and with such information as was available to them, they entered into a contract of that kind without knowing whether they could carry it out or not? I submit that they must be taken as knowing all about it. Do you suppose that this was an entirely new project ? Not at all. The question of summer and winter communication between the island and the mainland engaged the thoughts of many men. And when the people of Canada persuaded the people of the little island to cast in their lot with them, they must have known that they were bound to carry out this service, because aft most it only entailed a question of money. It would be grossly unfair and unjust for the people of the Dominion to say now to the people of Prince Edward Island, who relied upon the good faith of the government and the people of Canada to surrender their political independence to become a province of the Dominion ; I say it would be unfair and unjust for us to say now to the people of Prince Edward Island : We are going to change the terms of the compact which led you to agree to confederation; when we gave you this positive pledge we did not know what we were doing : we meant you to understand that we would carry out the contract only it it were reasonably possible to do so without any large expenditure ; we want you now to accept our interpretation of the contract. I say. Sir, that whatever may be the measure of damages which the people of the island are entitled to claim ; whether we have estimated it at too much or too little ; we are bound to implement the terms of the union in justice
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

maintopic: P. E. I. CLAIMS-MAINTENANCE OF STEAM COMMUNICATION.
speechtext: to the people of Prince Edward Island. We are bound to adequately and fairly compensate them for the losses they sustained during the years in which we failed to carry out our side of the bargain. The thought occurred to me that we were only giving fifty cents per capita of the population of the island for each year of the sixteen years that the service was defective, and I do not think that is an enormous amount. Any one who considers that a fair basis for making the allowance will have no hesitation in saying that a million dollars is a reasonable compensation to allow for the failure to carry out the contract on our part. We believe we have chosen the preferable course in paying to the people of the island the interest on one million dollars a year at 3 per cent, instead of handing over the capital to them to spend as they might choose. Under the circumstances, I would hope that there will be breadth enough of spirit in this House and in the country-even though hon. gentlemen opposite may think they can make a little political capital against us-to endorse the government of Canada in their action in carrying out the obligations of this great country with the small province of Prince Edward Island.

maintopic: P. E. I. CLAIMS-MAINTENANCE OF STEAM COMMUNICATION.
speechtext:
Hon. gentlemen opposite seem most desirous to thoroughly thresh out this question, and we are quite willing to accommodate them in that regard. What we contend for is, that there should be a finality to these claims, and that is the very thing that the Liberals contended for when they sat in opposition. We had a readjustment of the subsidies given to the provinces in 1884 ; we had another readjustment in 1887 by which we gave a certain amount yearly to Prince Edward Island, and we thought that was a settlement of all claims prior to that date. But, now we have another claim looming up. Well, as Mr. Blake said : There will be an end to confederation unless there is a finality to these claims. The Prime Minister tells us that whenever there is a just claim the government will always consider it, and the Minister of Finance says that the claims of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia were submitted under the precedent established in respect to the claims of Ontario and Quebec. Does the Minister of Finance understand the question at all ? The claims between Ontario and Quebec were adjudicated upon by this House, and the principle of the indebtedness settled. A certain sum of money was deducted annually from the payments made to Ontario and Quebec on account of some alleged indebtedness of these provinces to the Dominion, and under the readjustment of the subsidies in 1884, it only became a question of the division of the interest between Ontario and Quebec. It was on these grounds that the submission was made in the case of Ontario and Que-1 bee, and there is no comparision with this

ease at all, and no argument in favour of the same form of submission being adopted with respect to New Brunswick and Nova Scotia. What we are discussing at the present time is the granting of this large sum of money to Prince Edward Island, and we are taking the same grounds as were taken by the Liberal party when in opposition, and of which the hon. minister (Hon. Sir Louis Davies) was a distinguished supporter. Every man in this House supposed that by the Act of 1884, and the Act of 1887, as far as Prince Edward Island was concerned. there was a finality to these claims. We are not objecting to the sum to be given to Prince Edward Island. Not at all. The amount is a trifle to this Dominion. It is the principle of the thing we are objecting to. We are objecting to the introduction of measures of this kind again and again into this parliament, without the other provinces who are parties to the confederation being consulted. A system is being adopted by which the subsidies to the different provinces are fixed, giving to one province, perhaps, more than it is entitled to. and without consulting the wishes or the interests of the other provinces. That is what we object to. If it is necessary for the carrying on of the provincial governments that they should get more from the Dominion treasury, let there be a readjustment all along the line, but do not go on giving grants to particular provinces when every one believed that after 1884 there was an end to the claims of these provinces for such grants. In 1887, an Act was passed giving exceptional treatment to Prince Edward Island, and what has happened from 1887 down to the present day to entitle it to this 830.000 a year ? Must not the assumption be that in 1887 all the claims of Prince Edward Island were considered and finally dealt with, so far as an Act of parliament could do so? The Minister of Railways says that here we have an Act of parliament, and that is the end of it. WTell. have we not again and again gone behind the Subsidy Act whenever it was thought there was a claim in equity ? What I protest against on behalf of my province, and on behalf of the Dominion and its permanency as a confederation, is this continual tinkering and this giving of exceptional favours to different provinces. As Mr. Blake said long ago. there should have been a finality long before this ; but. if there are any claims which particular provinces have, or any ante-election promises which have to be carried out, let both sides of the House come to a solemn agreement, that if it is necessary to readjust the subsidies they shall be readjusted once for all. and that no claim on the part of any province shall be entertained afterwards. Otherwise, there must be an end to confederation.

maintopic: P. E. I. CLAIMS-MAINTENANCE OF STEAM COMMUNICATION.
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman's argument is based on an assumption of a set of
facts which does not exist. He assumes that this proposition involves a readjustment of the terms of confederation. He says that is a dangerous proposal to introduce into this House. He says that when the proposal in respect to Nova Scotia was introduced by the government of the late Sir John Macdonald, Mr. Blake protested against it, pointed out its danger, and contended . for finality. What is the sense of introducing such an argument here, when the proposal before the House has no reference whatever to a readjustment of the terms of union ? Does the hon. gentleman press his argument so far as to say that no claim made by any province on any ground shall ever be entertained by the Dominion, whether it is good, bad, or indifferent ? The hon. gentleman must see that he is taking a position which is absurd. We are not proposing to readjust the terms of confederation. We are not asking that an additional subsidy be given to any province. We are simply settling a claim for a specific amount, which claim we decide to be bona fide and good. The hon. gentleman has no objection to the amount of the settlement; but he imagines that in some way or other it is a readjustment of the terms of union, and therefore dangerous. Another lion, gentleman said this settlement had some political significance. I called on the hon. gentlemen who represent Prince County, east and west, who were in the House during the first part of this debate, and stayed here for an hour and a half, to answer that statement, and show their friends on that side of the House that there was not a vestige of foundation for it; and 1 am very sorry to see that on this matter, which is more vital to Prince Edward Island than anything that has come before the House for years
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

maintopic: P. E. I. CLAIMS-MAINTENANCE OF STEAM COMMUNICATION.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: P. E. I. CLAIMS-MAINTENANCE OF STEAM COMMUNICATION.
speechtext: This is a settlement of a just claim which has been pressed here for many years, and on which all political parties in Prince Edward Island are united; and just when we approached a crisis in the debate, the two hon. gentlemen from Prince Edward Island on the other side of the House, frightened at what their leader had said, withdrew themselves from the House altogether. I wanted these hon. gentlemen to respond to the invitation 1 gave them, and to tell my hon. friend from West York (Mr. Wallace) that he is entirely in error when he says that this proposal is the carrying out of any election promise or has any reference to party politics whatever. So far as I am concerned, it never formed a factor, direct or indirect, in the election on one side or the other.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
maintopic: P. E. I. CLAIMS-MAINTENANCE OF STEAM COMMUNICATION.
speechtext: There is the hon. member for West Prince (Mr. Hackett) now.

maintopic: P. E. I. CLAIMS-MAINTENANCE OF STEAM COMMUNICATION.
speechtext: I am glad lie lias come in. I liope my voice reached him, and I hope he will now let the hon. gentleman know that there is no ground whatever for the charge he makes, that the settlement of this claim is the result of any political agreement made between one party here and any party in Prince Edward Island. The claim was in existence before the Liberal party came into power; every Conservative in the island was pledged to it, every Conservative member from Prince Edward Island in this House was pledged to it. Those who went to petition the Queen on behalf of this claim were Conservatives; and the statement that this settlement is in liquidation of any political promise is absolutely devoid of fact. It has nothing whatever to do with politics; and I had hoped that the two lion, members from Prince Edward Island who support the opposition would have risen in their places and made the statement I asked them to make, that this is a settlement of a bona tide, honest claim, and is not in liquidation of any election promise, and has no reference to party politics whatever. I am glad to see one of those lion, gentleman back in his place now, and I want to know if he will make that statement ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

maintopic: P. E. I. CLAIMS-MAINTENANCE OF STEAM COMMUNICATION.
speechtext: I have only just arrived in the House this moment. I heard the early stages of the debate; but I understand that the lion. Minister of Marine and Fisheries has said in my absence that I was not here to attend to my duties as a member representing the Conservative party. Did the hon. gentleman say that ?

maintopic: P. E. I. CLAIMS-MAINTENANCE OF STEAM COMMUNICATION.
speechtext: I regretted very deeply that in one of the most important debates to Prince Edward Island which have taken place iu this House, the hon. gentleman withdrew himself before the debate was half over, and was out for an hour.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

maintopic: P. E. I. CLAIMS-MAINTENANCE OF STEAM COMMUNICATION.
speechtext: I was only out of the Chamber for about fifteen minutes; but I have listened carefully to the debate, because it is a matter of great importance to the people of Prince Edward Island, and I felt that our interests were safe in the hands of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries on this occasion.

maintopic: P. E. I. CLAIMS-MAINTENANCE OF STEAM COMMUNICATION.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: P. E. I. CLAIMS-MAINTENANCE OF STEAM COMMUNICATION.
speechtext:
In other debates of this kind the hon. gentleman himself has been absent. As I said on a previous occasion, this consideration which is given to the people of Prince Edward Island because of the non-fulfilment of the terms of union is only a moiety of what I believe the people of Prince Edward Island are entitled to. The party to which I belong, led in 1886 by the present Chief Justice of Prince Edward Island, the Hon. Mr. Sullivan, assisted by his Mr. TAYLOR.
able colleague, the present Hon. Senator Ferguson, finding that no relief was being afforded to the people of Prince Edward Island because of the non-fulfilment of those terms, carried the question to the foot of the Throne; and, as a result of that, the first real bona fide attempt to carry out the terms of confederation was made, and the steamer Stanley was placed on the route. Now, I had supposed at the outset of this debate that the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries, by his able remarks, had convinced the committee that the claim of Prince Edward Island was a just and fair one, and that the measure would pass without any great debate. I know that the hon. gentleman has behind him two supporters from Prince Edward Island. Are they in their seats, or are they absent V

maintopic: P. E. I. CLAIMS-MAINTENANCE OF STEAM COMMUNICATION.
speechtext: They are here.

maintopic: P. E. I. CLAIMS-MAINTENANCE OF STEAM COMMUNICATION.
speechtext: The appeal was made to me to correct the misunderstanding which the hon. gentleman's leader entertained and expressed.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

maintopic: P. E. I. CLAIMS-MAINTENANCE OF STEAM COMMUNICATION.
speechtext:
Sir, I have been here on every occasion during this session when my presence was required to assist in carrying out everything possible in the interests of the people of Canada, and 1 think it was a small matter for the bon. gentleman to refer to my absence for a short time on this occasion. I trust that there will be no further discussion on this matter. I remember well, from my long experience not only in political life in this House, but as a resident of Prince Edward Island, the great suffering entailed on the people of that province because of the non-fulfilment of the terms of union.
I can verify the truth of the statements made by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries with regard to the claim of Prince Edward Island. Why, in 1878-five years after the island had entered confederation under the solemn compact that she would be provided with continuous steam communication with the mainland-nothing had been done. When I crossed over the Straits of Northumberland for the first time in 1878, we had to drive in mid-winter in a sleigh from Emerald Junction, on the main line of the Prince Edward Island Railway, to Cape Traverse. Then we had to take the old iceboat, which had been in use there from time immemorial, to cross the straits, and then drive 35 or 40 miles until we came to the Intercolonial Railway. Surely this would not be called carrying out the terms of confederation. This condition of things was borne for many years. It was brought up repeatedly in parliament but nothing was done. I, myself, brought it up in parliament in 1881, but not getting any satisfaction from the government, then led by Sir John Macdonald, I stayed over a few days after prorogation and paid a special visit to Sir

John at his residence in this city, Stadacona Hall. I pointed out to him how vital a question this was to the island, and after I had laid before him the disadvantages under which we were labouring, he said to me : Hackett, at the time of confederation, when we entered into this contract with the island, we were not supposed to overcome the impossibilities of nature, but we will do all possible. And as a result of that visit, we had a railway built from Emerald Junction to Cape Traverse and thus had only the short passage across the straits to overcome in order to reach the Intercolonial Railway.
The claim of Prince Edward Island for $5,000,000 was made to this government over and over again by Chief Justice Sullivan and Mr. Ferguson. Senator Howland did what he could to have a tunnel built, but without success, and Lord Granville declared that something should be done for the people of the island.
In 1888 the Stanley was placed on the route. The hon. the Minister of Marine has said that the Northern Light did not fulfil the contract. Neither she did. The placing of the Stanley on the route was the first genuine attempt to carry out the terms of the union. Since the present government have come into power, they have placed the Minto on the route, and she has to some extent assisted in carrying out the terms of confederation. But unless you place these boats at the particular points from which they can navigate the straits on all occasions, you cannot have continuous communication. You have two powerful steamers, built for the purpose of ice navigation, but you have them both at the one point, where the passage is blocked when the winds blow from the north-east. If you had one at the western point plying between Summerside and Cape Tormentine, she at all times could be used when the eastern channel was blocked. You may call the present system satisfactory, if you like, but during twelve days this session, in the month of February, we were without our mails. Is that carrying out the terms of the union? I trust that this Bill will pass without further discussion. It is only a small payment of what is due the people.
With regard to the tax on commercial travellers, which was referred to by the hon. member for East Toronto (Mr. Kemp), that was imposed by the friends of the Minister of Marine who are now in power on the island. When in Charlottetown, a few years ago, a commercial traveller from Halifax was not acquainted with the law and did not pay the fee. What happened ? In came a policeman with a detective appointed by the local government and they arrested this man in the hotel and put him in jail. This tax is altogether wrong, and it is to be hoped that the people of one province will not be impeded in their dealings with other provinces by this vexatious tax.
I simply rose to resent the attempt made by the hon. Minister of Marine to detract from my standing as a member of this House because I happened to be absent for a few minutes on this occasion.

maintopic: P. E. I. CLAIMS-MAINTENANCE OF STEAM COMMUNICATION.
speechtext: I may say on behalf of my hon. friend, who has just spoken, that during the present session he has been in the House at least twice as much as the Minister of Marine, and I do not think that any reproach, such as the Minister of Marine has made, comes with good grace from a government which has not an average of more than two or three of its members in the House, as a usual thing.

maintopic: P. E. I. CLAIMS-MAINTENANCE OF STEAM COMMUNICATION.
speechtext: Is not always the position of a cabinet minister exceedingly difficult? He is called out of the House continuously, and it is perhaps practically impossible for him to spend any length of time in the House, owing to the many demands made upon his time.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

maintopic: P. E. I. CLAIMS-MAINTENANCE OF STEAM COMMUNICATION.
speechtext:
There is a very great deal in what the hon. minister has said, and no doubt there is a great deal of necessity for the ministers at the head of Railways and Canals and Public Works absenting themselves, but other members have demands on their time as well, and it certainly came with very bad grace from the Minister of Marine to make the reflections he did on my hon. friend, who is a most assidu-out attendant at the debates.
I would like to say to the Minister of Railways and Canals that when he tells us we should have had the information about the vote which is to be passed in respect of the province of New Brunswick, he ought to have borne in mind that we only knew to-day for the first time that any application was to be made to parliament for that vote. I think the Minister of Finance will see the necessity of bringing the papers down and having them printed, so that the information may be in the possession of the House. When parliament is asked to vote this sum for New Brunswick-and I may support the vote myself-we want to know something about it. And so does every hon. member of this House. Every hon. member is entitled to know the facts before he is asked to vote for it And, if the government intend to propose this appropriation during this session, they should have brought the papers down and had them printed But, this not having been done, I will ask the government to do it with the least possible delay.

maintopic: P. E. I. CLAIMS-MAINTENANCE OF STEAM COMMUNICATION.
speechtext:
On that latter point, I may say that I supposed that these papers had been brought down. The fact of the two awards having been made has been referred to in debate several times during the present session, so that there has been no lack of knowledge of the fact

that these awards would have to be provided for. As soon as I learned that the papers had not been brought down I sent instructions to my department that, in whatever department these papers were, that they should be produced at once.

maintopic: P. E. I. CLAIMS-MAINTENANCE OF STEAM COMMUNICATION.
speechtext:
I may say that the claims themselves and the papers connected with them, except the last, the award of the arbitrators itself have been in the journals over and over again. Therefore, there will be nothing new to hon. members in the papers except the finding of the arbitrators.
Bill reported, read the third time, and passed.

maintopic: ELECTRIC LIGHT INSPECTION.

speechtext:
Bill (No. 140) to amend the Electric Light Inspection Act-the Minister of Inland Revenue (Hon. M. E. Bernier) read the second time, and House went into committee thereon.
On section 3,

maintopic: ELECTRIC LIGHT INSPECTION.
speechtext: I am not familiar with the Act which is being amended. Is this Act applicable throughout Canada, and does it apply to the ordinary supply of electric light by companies in cities throughout Canada ?

maintopic: ELECTRIC LIGHT INSPECTION.
speechtext: Throughout Canada. There are inspectors in all the cities under this Act. There is one in Halifax.

maintopic: ELECTRIC LIGHT INSPECTION.
speechtext: It is the duty of these inspectors to verify all meters before they go into use ?

maintopic: ELECTRIC LIGHT INSPECTION.
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: ELECTRIC LIGHT INSPECTION.
speechtext: Whether they are asked to do so or not ?

maintopic: ELECTRIC LIGHT INSPECTION.
speechtext: They are never installed unless they are tested.

maintopic: ELECTRIC LIGHT INSPECTION.
speechtext: I mean, if a meter is put into a House, is it a necessary condition that it shall be inspected before- hand by an officer under this Act 1

maintopic: ELECTRIC LIGHT INSPECTION.
speechtext:
Yes.
On section 5,

maintopic: ELECTRIC LIGHT INSPECTION.
speechtext: I do not quite understand what the object of this section is. It seems to be exactly the same as that which was passed a few minutes ago. Why do you confine the time to three months ?

maintopic: ELECTRIC LIGHT INSPECTION.
speechtext: The accounts are generally rendered at the end of three months. I think that time is fair to both consumer and seller.

maintopic: ELECTRIC LIGHT INSPECTION.
speechtext: I think that is a very wise clause. When the inspector goes around, and if he finds there is anything wrong with the meter, the purchaser always wants a rebate ever since the inspector was there last.

maintopic: ELECTRIC LIGHT INSPECTION.
speechtext: He does not get it.

maintopic: ELECTRIC LIGHT INSPECTION.
speechtext: There should be a time limit, and I think three months is ample. I may say to those who think that the customers are often being shaved by the companies, that the difficulty is all on the other side. If there is anything wrong with the meter it is not because it goes too fast, but because it goes too slow. That is a notorious fact, and it is the man who is selling electric light that gets taken in and not the purchaser, because something will get on the disk and retard the movement. In fact, we find that parties who take the current sometimes tamper with the meter. I think three months as the date from which rebate should be made is ample for all purposes.

maintopic: ELECTRIC LIGHT INSPECTION.
speechtext: It seems to me that the amount of time which should be given under a section of this kind must depend to a great extent on the frequency of the inspection. For example, if you had not had your meter inspected for a great many months, it might be that three months would be too short a time. W'ould the hon. gentleman tell us whether any specific periods are fixed by the Act now being amended for the inspection of these meters ?

maintopic: ELECTRIC LIGHT INSPECTION.
speechtext: The inspection is regulated by law at five years, and if any person casts doubt upon the regularity of the meter, he may ask the inspector to test his meter, and that is why we have fixed the period at three months, because the payments are generally made by the consumer every three months.

maintopic: ELECTRIC LIGHT INSPECTION.
speechtext: I do not see that the time of payment has really very much to do with it, but, it seems to me that the frequency of inspection has a great deal to do with it. Is there any fee fixed for the inspection ? How much does it cost to have a meter inspected ?

maintopic: ELECTRIC LIGHT INSPECTION.
speechtext:
Here is a list of fees as fixed according to the regulations adopted in 1895 :
For meters of a capacity of tea ligths or under, 75 cents ; for a capacity of over ten lights and unler 20, $1.25 ; for 20 and under 30, $1.75 ; far 30 and under 45, $2.25 ; for 45 and under 60, $2.75 ; for 60 and under 80, $3.00 ; 80 and under 100, $3.50 and for every additionnal 20 lights, 50 cents.

maintopic: ELECTRIC LIGHT INSPECTION.
speechtext: I do not understand these technical expressions very well. How much would it cost to have an inspection of the ordinary meter, such as one has in his house ?

maintopic: ELECTRIC LIGHT INSPECTION.
speechtext: It costs 75 cents for the ordinary -meter, and it must be paid by the electric company, not by the consumer.

maintopic: ELECTRIC LIGHT INSPECTION.
speechtext:
I think six months would be fairer a-s far as it concerns the consumer, because if the company has to pay it, it is only in very infrequent cases, and it will not be much of a loss if the meter is running against the consumer. There is in reality three months now. I think that a remission of six months should be allowed.

On section 5,

maintopic: ELECTRIC LIGHT INSPECTION.
speechtext: This is the section which I think there may be some difficulty about. For example, supposing that any one conceived that his meter was wrong, and wrote to tiie inspector and asked him to come and inspect the meter, and the electric light manager knew nothing about it. The Bill says that either one or the other, the inspector or the person applying for the inspection, should give notice. Suppose the consumer told the inspector that lie had notified us. and the inspector thought he had, when, in reality, we knew nothing about it. That would put the onus upon us, whereas we would not be cognizant of what was going on. It seems to me that it should be made the duty of, either the inspector, or of the person applying, to give the notice.

maintopic: ELECTRIC LIGHT INSPECTION.
speechtext: Twenty-four hours notice will be given to the contractor, or his agent, by both of the parties interested.

maintopic: ELECTRIC LIGHT INSPECTION.
speechtext: I understand that, but, suppose the inspector is told by the consumer that he has given us notice when he has not, one would throw the blame on the other, and we would not know anything about it. Either one or the other should be obliged to give the notice, and not leave it for two of them in that way.

maintopic: ELECTRIC LIGHT INSPECTION.
speechtext:
I think the section seems to be very clear. The hon. gentleman complains of the delay. It says :
During the inspection of any disputed meter, the contractor or purchaser may be present by himself or his agent authorized in writing.

maintopic: ELECTRIC LIGHT INSPECTION.
speechtext: That is all right.

maintopic: ELECTRIC LIGHT INSPECTION.
speechtext: And twenty-four hours notice of the inspection shall be given, by the inspector or person at whose request the inspection is made, to the other party.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
maintopic: ELECTRIC LIGHT INSPECTION.
speechtext: I would suggest that you make it read ' twenty-four hours notice shall be given by the inspector,' striking out the words ' or person at whose request the inspection is made.'

maintopic: ELECTRIC LIGHT INSPECTION.
speechtext: I suppose the consumer would be the party to complain, and notice must be given to him by the inspector as well as the contractor. or if the consumer gives the notice to the company, then, the same notice should be given to the contractor. Both parties must be notified.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
maintopic: ELECTRIC LIGHT INSPECTION.
speechtext:
But, you make the inspector, or the person who complains, responsible for giving the notice. The person who makes the complaint may tell the inspector that he has given notice to the contractor without giving it. If you hold your own officer responsible for giving the notice and Mr. MACLEAN.
strike out the words ' or person at whose request the inspection is made,' the notice will then be given by the inspector.

maintopic: ELECTRIC LIGHT INSPECTION.
speechtext: Yes, we might say * by the inspector to both parties interested.'

maintopic: ELECTRIC LIGHT INSPECTION.
speechtext: I would like to ask the hon. gentleman if there is anything in this Bill, or the original Act, that applies to companies supplying light where there is no meter at all ?

maintopic: ELECTRIC LIGHT INSPECTION.
speechtext: Where there is no meter, there can be no inspection.

maintopic: ELECTRIC LIGHT INSPECTION.
speechtext: Do I understand that a company has the right to supply electric light in a town, and that the government make no inspection of the electric light planr ?

maintopic: ELECTRIC LIGHT INSPECTION.
speechtext: If a citizen in a town takes electric light from a company without a meter, of course, we have nothing to do with ilmt except to register the company. Where there is no meter there can be no inspection, and no supervision, except the registration of the company.

maintopic: ELECTRIC LIGHT INSPECTION.
speechtext: With all due deference the minister is a little wrong on that. We have to give every new customer a notice in writing of the amount of pressure we are going to deliver at the terminus in his house. If we do not deliver that pressure he can have the inspector test as to whether we are giving that pressure or not.

maintopic: ELECTRIC LIGHT INSPECTION.
speechtext: Not having any meter.

maintopic: ELECTRIC LIGHT INSPECTION.
speechtext: Not having any meter. When we sell power on the flat, we have to give a certain amount of pressure so that when a man has a sixteen candle power light in his house, he will get a sixteen candle power light.

maintopic: ELECTRIC LIGHT INSPECTION.
speechtext: Do I understand that an electric company can make a contract with a municipal corporation to supply electric light, and run for ten years without the government making an inspection ?

maintopic: ELECTRIC LIGHT INSPECTION.
speechtext: If they think they are not getting the required pressure, all they have to do is to inform the inspector and he will see whether it is right or not.

maintopic: ELECTRIC LIGHT INSPECTION.
speechtext:
One would think that there should be a regular inspection.
On section 6,

maintopic: ELECTRIC LIGHT INSPECTION.
speechtext: This clause inflicts a very severe penalty, and we should like to know the reason for it.

maintopic: ELECTRIC LIGHT INSPECTION.
speechtext: The meters are fixed by our inspector, and it is in order to prevent any person from interfering or tampering with these meters that the penalty is provided.

maintopic: ELECTRIC LIGHT INSPECTION.
speechtext: It does not say anything about ' tampering ' with the meter. Suppose the inspector lives a long distance away, and I am not satisfied that I am getting the proper pressure-

maintopic: ELECTRIC LIGHT INSPECTION.
speechtext: Speak a little louder; I cannot hear you.

maintopic: ELECTRIC LIGHT INSPECTION.
speechtext: I will have to borrow the voice of the Minister of Customs (Hon. Mr. Paterson).

maintopic: ELECTRIC LIGHT INSPECTION.
speechtext: If you prevent those people speaking here I may be able to hear.

maintopic: ELECTRIC LIGHT INSPECTION.
speechtext: It is the disorder of my bon. friend's neighbours that prevents his hearing. I say that it is very arbitrary to provide a fine of $25 on any person who tests a meter. The customer may believe that he is not getting the light he purchased, and if some competent person in the neighbourhood tests the meter I do not see why he should be punished. Of course, If any one tampers with the meter so as to cause it to register less power, then a penalty ought to be provided, but this clause as it reads is arbitrary and unnecessary. Then, as regards the question raised by the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Blainf as to where there are no meters. If you are paying for a twenty candle power light, the government should see that you get it as well as if you had a meter. I protest against the unnecessary hardship of this clause which provides a penalty on a person who may do no wrong, except to test the meter.

maintopic: ELECTRIC LIGHT INSPECTION.
speechtext: I think this is one of the very best clauses in this Bill, and for this reason. It frequently happens that fakers from a distance who have neither money nor conscience, tell customers that their meters are all wrong when such is not the case, with the hope of getting some money consideration. The idea is to have authorized inspectors to inspect these meters. All that any of our customers has to do is to send for the government inspector who thoroughly understands the business. The number of watts a customer consumes is given to him on a piece of paper with the dials, and if he thinks his meter is running too fast or too slow, all he has to do is to get the inspector to inspect the meter, and the man who furnishes the light has to pay for it. The consumer is amply protected. So far as those who get the current on the flat are concerned, if they think they are not getting the proper candle power, all they have to do is to write to the inspector and he will see to it.

maintopic: ELECTRIC LIGHT INSPECTION.
speechtext: The hon. member for Renfrew (Mr. Wright) is looking after the interests of the electric light companies. I was speaking in the interest of the general public.

maintopic: ELECTRIC LIGHT INSPECTION.
speechtext: They are amply protected.

maintopic: ELECTRIC LIGHT INSPECTION.
speechtext: Of course the hon. gentleman (Mr. Wright) can make out a very admirable case for the electric light companies, but our experience is that these companies gobble up everything in sight and charge rates that are very high, and in addition to that we have no certainty that they are giving us what we pay for. The hon. member says : Oh, you can send for the inspector, and all that. In a city like Ottawa, the inspector may be right at hand, but it may be difficult to get an inspector in some country places. By the way, does the inspector perform this duty for nothing?

maintopic: ELECTRIC LIGHT INSPECTION.
speechtext: The company and not the consumer has to pay.

maintopic: ELECTRIC LIGHT INSPECTION.
speechtext: If the consumer is aggrieved, he sends for the inspector and the company pays ?

maintopic: ELECTRIC LIGHT INSPECTION.
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: ELECTRIC LIGHT INSPECTION.
speechtext: That is a very good provision. I raise the other point that there may be a competent man near at hand to test your line, and that there should not be a penalty imposed on him if he does that.

maintopic: ELECTRIC LIGHT INSPECTION.
speechtext: Twenty-four hours will bring an inspector at any time.

maintopic: ELECTRIC LIGHT INSPECTION.
speechtext: The whole object of this is to protect the public, and the public are protected by providing proper government inspection. The cases alluded to by the hon. member for West York, where people feel themselves aggrieved and desire some one to test their meter, often create trouble. There have been a great many attempts at blackmailing in matters of this kind, and the companies desire to see the inspection placed under a proper government inspection. The case cannot arise where a government inspector cannot be had. Any person who feels himself aggrieved can have an inspector, and at the expense of the company. I do not see why you should object to it at all.

maintopic: ELECTRIC LIGHT INSPECTION.
speechtext: I would like to ask the minister a question. The statement has been made a couple of times, and I would like it verified by the minister, that an inspector is sent for, and the electric light company pays his expenses. Is that correct?

maintopic: ELECTRIC LIGHT INSPECTION.
speechtext: The electric light company does not pay his travelling expenses, but it pays the inspection of the meter.

maintopic: ELECTRIC LIGHT INSPECTION.
speechtext: If the meter after being tested is right, the consumer has to pay for the inspection. If it is wrong, the company which is responsible for the meter has to pay the expense.

maintopic: ELECTRIC LIGHT INSPECTION.
speechtext:
Now we have got a little more light on it. We have a direct

contradiction by the minister of the statement made by the hon. member for Renfrew (Mr. Wright). The hon. member for Renfrew said that all you have to do if you are aggrieved is to send for the inspector, and he comes, and the company pays the expense. Now we are informed by the minister-but he did not give us the information when he heard the statement made, but rather left us to force it from him-that if the inspection proves that the consumer is getting what he is bargaining for, then he has to pay the expense. But there is the other difficulty. You send for the inspector. The company know that the inspector is in town, and they put on the very strongest light they can; but is that any assurance that for the previous month the consumer has been getting what he bought and has to pay for?

maintopic: ELECTRIC LIGHT INSPECTION.
speechtext: I would like to point out, for the information of the hon. member for West York, that when you complain of your meter, and it is inspected, you are allowed under this Bill to have your representative present, so that to that extent there is some protection to the public. But I have not yet been told why this new penalty is introduced. Supposing I am a consumer of electric light, and I ask the best expert in Canada, or a man like Mr. Edison, to inspect my meter. I can only do so by subjecting him to this penalty. It is true, some fakirs have come into town ; but they only did so after they found that the consumers of electric light had been charged exorbitant rates, and that meters were over-measuring. While I am thoroughly in accord with the regulations made, providing the consumer may have a representative present at the inspection, I would like the minister to give a reason why this new penalty has been put in the Act.

maintopic: ELECTRIC LIGHT INSPECTION.
speechtext:
It may be that the statement made by the hon. member for East York (Mr. Maclean) explains the question which he has asked. I have heard, as he has, of the gentlemen whom he has spoken of as fakirs, coming into Toronto and testing meters. I have also heard it stated that these meters were of such a delicate nature that with a magnet the whole meter could, in a few seconds, be thrown out. Whether that is correct or not the minister can tell us. Therefore, the neces-! sity for a government inspection. A meter cannot be placed in a house unless it bears a government stamp. If that was wise legislation for the protection not only of the company, but of the public, it necessarily follows, I should say, that mat government stamped meter must be protected, and I assume that it is because a meter can be thrown out in such a way, by men who are fakirs, so that it will not correctly report Mr. WALLACE.
what amount of light has been consumed, that the government have determined to make the government inspection paramount, a heavy penalty is therefore imposed on other people who inspect meters.

maintopic: ELECTRIC LIGHT INSPECTION.
speechtext: With regard to the question of the hon. member for West York, I would refer him to section 19 of the Act as it stands at present.

maintopic: ELECTRIC LIGHT INSPECTION.
speechtext: Will the minister tell us why he has put this penalty on the public? Is the statement made by the hon, member for North Simcoe (Mr. McCarthy) correct?

maintopic: ELECTRIC LIGHT INSPECTION.
speechtext: Yes, quite correct.

maintopic: ELECTRIC LIGHT INSPECTION.
speechtext: That these fakirs can demoralize a meter?

maintopic: ELECTRIC LIGHT INSPECTION.
speechtext: Yes. The hon. member will understand that I have no personal knowledge of that, but the information has been conveyed to me.

maintopic: ELECTRIC LIGHT INSPECTION.
speechtext: On whose statement?

maintopic: ELECTRIC LIGHT INSPECTION.
speechtext: I may say that one of these meters is one of the most delicate pieces of mechanism you Can find. It runs on jewels, and a strong blow will put it out of order.

maintopic: ELECTRIC LIGHT INSPECTION.
