I am very glad to hear that, and I am sure that the business men throughout the country will be delighted to know that we are not going to have any more twenty-cent pieces in circulation. I wish that the minister could adopt some means by which the twenty-cent coin now in circulation would be withdrawn. If it could be declared that in six months or a year the twenty-cent piece will cease to be a legal tender, or if in some other way it could be forced out of circulation, the business people of Canada would be very thankful to the Minister of Finance. Then I assume that the coins will be 5, 10, 25 and 50-cent pieces. I am not very, favourably impressed with the silver dollar. The MINISTER OF FINANCE. I do not want to speak definitely about the dollar. It is worth considering. Mr. HENDERSON. I think a gold dollar coin is too small for Canada. The MINISTER OF FINANCE. I am glad to say that I agree with almost every word my hon. friend has uttered. He is probably not aware that we have not made any 20-cent pieces in Canada since confederation. The 20-cent piece is a nuisance, but any one who examines it will see that it is a Newfoundland coin. Mr. MACLEAN. I had two yesterday. The MINISTER OF FINANCE. They must have known that my hon. friend had silver on the brain. Mr. MACLEAN. I gave them to a blind man. The MINISTER OF FINANCE. Did you give them for quarters ? Mr. MACLEAN. No. The MINISTER OF FINANCE. The government of Newfoundland adhere to the 20-cent piece. I wish they would not, because it leads to a great deal of embarrassment. With regard to American silver, I am not sure that it can be got rid of as easily as my hon. friend supposes. If any means can be devised by which it can be replaced by Canadian silver, we shall be very glad to adopt them. Mr. MACLEAN. What are the denominations of the gold coins ? The MINISTER OF FINANCE. We have not worked that out yet. The $5, unquestionably, the half sovereign, or its equivalent. $2.50, and the $10. I do not think we shall go above the $10 gold piece. Mr. MACLEAN. The hon. gentleman might find an outlet for the Canadian sovereigns if the British government would have their sovereigns for the fleets on the Atlantic and the Pacific minted in Canada. The MINISTER OF FINANCE. The sovereign which we make in Ottawa will be current legal tender in any country where

the British flag flies, and will naturally be taken in any part of the world.

maintopic: THE ROYAL MINT.
speechtext: It appears to me that the circulation of American silver is a very serious evil, and I think it arises from the fact that a great deal of that silver comes into the country through different channels and is kept in circulation because it passes among the people without discount, while, if you seek to deposit it, the banks charge discount on it. If the lion. Finance Minister would consider whether some means might not be devised to have the banks redeem that silver at par, and then have it removed from the country, it seems to me that would make the way clear for the circulation of our own Canadian silver.

maintopic: THE ROYAL MINT.
speechtext: I will tell the minister one way in which it can be regulated. I know that there are agencies at work which bring in American silver in thousands of dollars by the boats coming to Toronto, and by other means, in order to get it circulated in Canada. There should be some way by which that silver should be made to come through the custom-house.

maintopic: THE ROYAL MINT.
speechtext: There is a very simple way by which it could be got rid of. The party to whom it is offered might refuse to take it.

maintopic: THE ROYAL MINT.
speechtext: You cannot.

maintopic: THE ROYAL MINT.
speechtext: You can. It is not a legal tender. The circulation of American silver in Canada is one of the incidents of our close relations with the United States. Along the border, and wherever a railway crosses the line, you will have large amounts of American silver coming in, and if you cleared it out one week, I am afraid you would find it there again the next week.

maintopic: THE ROYAL MINT.
speechtext: We know that there is a large profit in converting silver into coin, and if you gave a little better value by making your silver coins a little heavier than American silver, the Americans would take it in preference to their own, and in that way you would get a very large circulation. There is a profit of from 25 per cent to 30 per cent at the present time in the coinage of silver, so that you might get rid of the difficulty suggested by the hon. member for East York and give a great deal of work to your mint by giving a little better value in your coin. And I do not know but it would be a good idea, because if you could get into circulation in the United States several millions of dollars of Canadian silver, the Canadian mines and the Canadian mint would get the advantage.

maintopic: THE ROYAL MINT.
speechtext:
I wish to congratulate the government and the people of Canada on the measure that has been brought in to-day. As a Canadian, I feel a thrill of pleasure to find that we, ourselves, are at last going to make the money which we use Mr. FIELDING.
in this country. It is not given to everybody in this country to use $1 and $5 bills, but it is given to almost everybody to use the coppers, the 5-cent pieces and the quarters, and when we have our own Canadian stamp on the money of the country, we feel that we are part of the empire, and a thrill of patriotism runs through us. As the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Henderson) says, the 20-cent pieces are a perfect nuisance, and the government should call in every one of them. They cause a great deal of disturbance in giving change, they are so near the size of the quarter. Then, the mutilated coins cause a great deal of trouble. In my business we get thousands of small coins- five and ten-cent pieces and quarters-which are in such a mutilated condition that it is impossible to read them and tell their significance. When we get the new mint, I presume the government will pay special attention to these points, and will give us a clean coinage fit for the people to handle, and such as they will be proud of. We know the difficulty we have with the paper currency. A great many of the bills we get are so dirty that they are not fit to handle. These things should be corrected. I am glad that the government has brought in this measure.

maintopic: THE ROYAL MINT.
speechtext: I hope the minister will say that he is in favour of the issue of a silver dollar, which will give the country an incidental profit and a clean coinage. I am not arguing for a depreciated currency, but there is no reason why, instead of these dirty paper bills, the government should not Issue a clean silver dollar and plenty of them.

maintopic: THE ROYAL MINT.
speechtext: The various coins to be issued are a matter for consideration. I am not giving any final decision to-day.

maintopic: THE ROYAL MINT.
speechtext: What about the very practical suggestion of the hon. member for Westmoreland (Mr. Emmerson)? Cannot the minister suggest some means by which American silver can be redeemed at par at the different banks throughout the country ?

maintopic: THE ROYAL MINT.
speechtext: I would not care to answer off-hand. The great railways have a means of disposing of American currency, but I do not wish to incur any needless expense. We want to get any profit there is in this matter ourselves, and not give it to other people. However, the whole discussion has been very profitable, and I will take care that It receives every consideration in my department.

maintopic: THE ROYAL MINT.
speechtext:
This is a very difficult question, because the customs of the people with regard to American silver are greatly localized. The banks along the border take it at par.
Mr: MACLEAN. On the other side Canadian silver is refused, although we take American coinage all over Canada. I

was in an American city the other day, when a telegraph operator implored me to take a Canadian quarter, which, he said, had been passed in upon him, and he could not get rid of it.

maintopic: THE ROYAL MINT.
speechtext: I quite agree in what the hon member for East York has said. His remarks can be applied not only to silver, but to Canadian paper money as well. On many occasions in the last fifteen years, when travelling in the states I have strongly resented the conduct of our American neighbours with reference to our money. Practically in New York there is no place where they will take Canadian money-either Dominion currency or bank notes or silver-except at a discount.

maintopic: THE ROYAL MINT.
speechtext: They take it at the Waldorf.

maintopic: THE ROYAL MINT.
speechtext:
That is probably the only hotel where they will take Canadian money and not charge a discount. Go to the shops on Broadway or in Buffalo, Chicago or anywhere on the Pacific coast or elsewhere in the American union and they will not look at Canadian money. It is a source of humiliation and of great inconvenience to Canadians travelling in the United States that our money, particularly paper money, which is equivalent to gold; in value, should be refused in exchange for the American silver currency, the real value of which is only about sixty seven cents in the dollar. I do not know if there is any remedy, but I think it is a matter to which the hon. Minister of Finance might very well direct his attention.
Resolution reported, read the second time, and agreed to.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 143) for the establishment and maintenance in Canada of the Ottawa branch of the Royal Mint.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

maintopic: OCEAN STEAMSHIP SUBSIDIES.

speechtext: Bill (No. 141) further to amend the Act relating to ocean steamship subsidies (Hon. Sir Richard Cartwright) read the second time and House went into committee thereon.

maintopic: OCEAN STEAMSHIP SUBSIDIES.
speechtext: Is it intended that these steamers shall call at any other but a French port ?

maintopic: OCEAN STEAMSHIP SUBSIDIES.
speechtext: Under the terms of the French law, they must ply between Canadian and French ports. I am not certain whether the French government will object in case they touch at a Spanish port, but I rather think we would have to confine their voyages to French ports and ports of French colonies.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

maintopic: OCEAN STEAMSHIP SUBSIDIES.
speechtext:
What French ports will
they touch at?

maintopic: OCEAN STEAMSHIP SUBSIDIES.
speechtext: In northern France at Havre or Boulogne-probably Havre. In the Mediterranean at Marseilles.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

maintopic: OCEAN STEAMSHIP SUBSIDIES.
speechtext: Are you going to have two lines?

maintopic: OCEAN STEAMSHIP SUBSIDIES.
speechtext: We are desirous of cultivating the Mediterranean trade, and it may be found expedient to have a terminus in the Mediterranean as well as in north France. During the winter it may be found convenient that the steamers should go to the Mediterranean. The majority of the trips will be made to northern France, at the port of Havre.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

maintopic: OCEAN STEAMSHIP SUBSIDIES.
speechtext: To what ports does the trade of Canada go now?

maintopic: OCEAN STEAMSHIP SUBSIDIES.
speechtext: Our exports are comparatively small, about $1,400,000. They go chiefly to northern France. We are not doing very much in the Mediterranean. Our exports consist of agricultural imjflements and a certain amount of timber, besides breadstuffs and miscellaneous productions. We send a considerable quantity of fish, and that is perhaps the largest individual item. It consists largely of canned lobsters. It is a very pleasant experience to me to find that our fruits are so well received in France, and I hope we may extend our exports of fruits. Agricultural implements are the next largest item, and we have considerable hopes of that business being extended. The next largest item is wood. The miscellaneous items are very small : breadstuffs, $313,000 ; fish of all kinds, $520,000 ; agricultural implements. $208,000; lumber, about $190,000. That covers the present exports to France. I mentioned the other day that we hoped to develop a considerable trade in the matter of pulp. We also hope to speedily develop, particularly in the Mediterranean sections, a considerable trade in coal. My attention has been called to that point for a considerable time. I have always been of opinion that, with the extraordinary facilities for shipping coal from our Nova Scotia collieries, we should certainly be able to drive a considerable trade in coal. Iron, of course, is an experiment. But I judge from the information I have received there is a fair chance of being able to command a considerable trade in the export of iron.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

maintopic: OCEAN STEAMSHIP SUBSIDIES.
speechtext: Among the articles to go in under the most favoured tariff clause in this arrangement with France were live eels. Can the hon. minister tells us if there is a prospect of the extension of that trade ?

maintopic: OCEAN STEAMSHIP SUBSIDIES.
speechtext:
I am afraid that that trade remains tolerably stationary. I believe it was Sir

Charles Tupper who negotiated this. However, it is only fair to say that until the establishment of a direct line, the French treaty has had no fair chance, because, as I mentioned, the surtax, as it is called, renders it difficult to extend trade with France except directly. There is no doubt that if we could once get our goods introduced amongst the 40,000,000 people in France we have a good chance of developing trade. I think that the money spent by us last year will produce ^results in various indirect ways. I do not anticipate any large immigration from France, for our French friends are too fond [DOT]of their own country. But I think there is [DOT]a good chance, as was stated, of introducing large quantities of French capital into Canada. France is undoubtedly one of the richest countries in the world. Any one who has paid attention to financial movements knows that any enterprises that have been going on in Russia for many years past have been carried on largely by means of capital furnished from France. This is a point to which attention may well be paid. I am in hopes that we shall be able to extend not only in the lines I have mentioned but also to extend commerce in certain articles of food. I mentioned also that we are in hopes of receiving, semi-officially only, a visit from a gentleman who has been closely connected with the French government, and we hope to obtain some better arrangements, though the establishment of a steamship line is an indispensible preliminary.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

maintopic: OCEAN STEAMSHIP SUBSIDIES.
speechtext: So far as concerns the imports from France, which are a considerable sum, I do not know that it would be the duty of the government to specially concern themselves. Each country will find its customers in Canada and will supply them. What we are concerned with is in finding markets for the products of our country. So that in estimating the subsidy that is to be given we are confined, as the minister has confined the case, to a discussion of the exports from Canada to France. The value of our exports to France last year was $1,374,000. But the trade is decreasing ; the year before, it -was a considerable larger amount, $1,557,000.

maintopic: OCEAN STEAMSHIP SUBSIDIES.
speechtext: But if the hon. gentleman will look back to 1896, he will see that the exports then were only $580,000.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

maintopic: OCEAN STEAMSHIP SUBSIDIES.
speechtext:
But the imports from France in 1896 were only $2,800,000, instead of $4,368,000 as they were last year. Thus the increase of our imports has been $1,500,000 while the increase of our exports has been $800,000. The percentage of exports is larger but the amounts are smaller. But this seems to me to be a very large sum of money to pay to benefit a trade $1,374,000. The government would need to have in sight a very considerable market for the products of Canada before concluding a bar-
Sir RICHARD CARTWRI3HT.
gain to give a subsidy of $170,000 for such a meagre trade. No doubt the minister looks for a largely increased trade, especially in pullp, or, better still, in paper, because 1 think we should bend our efforts to exporting paper instead of pulp. The same machinery and water powers required for the production of pulp are required for the production of paper. I hope the minister will give us good returns next year for this very large expenditure, which could not be justified unless they are able to point next year to tangible results.

maintopic: OCEAN STEAMSHIP SUBSIDIES.
speechtext: I am in hopes that that may be the ease, but at the same time I may call the attention of the hon. gentleman and the House to this-in establishing a trade in European countries where they are not quite as receptive of new ideas as in younger countries, we must not expect results within year and day. We will do our best to obtain them. But, up to the present time, without a subsidized line of steamers it has been impossible to look for a very large increased trade.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

maintopic: OCEAN STEAMSHIP SUBSIDIES.
speechtext: Is it the intention of the government to follow this up by sending commercial agents to introduce Canadian goods ?

maintopic: OCEAN STEAMSHIP SUBSIDIES.
speechtext: Yes.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

maintopic: OCEAN STEAMSHIP SUBSIDIES.
speechtext: That is a complimentary measure without which there would be very little returns for our money. Another thing I would like to ask the minister is whether, if the ships of this subsidized line call at an English port on their way to France the Canadian goods in the cargo will be allowed to enter France under the lower tariff.

maintopic: OCEAN STEAMSHIP SUBSIDIES.
speechtext: My impression is that they are not allowed to touch at an English port.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

maintopic: OCEAN STEAMSHIP SUBSIDIES.
speechtext: Either in coming or going ?

maintopic: OCEAN STEAMSHIP SUBSIDIES.
speechtext: In returning I think they can, but not in going.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

maintopic: OCEAN STEAMSHIP SUBSIDIES.
speechtext: It is the intention of the company to have six steamers, three British and three French. The French subsidy operates automatically. The moment the steamers are built in France, they carry the subsidy. Now, with regard to the question whether a French steamer can call at other ports-I cannot say as to coming out to Canada. But I know the outgoing steamers from Canada to France, in order to have the benefit, not of the lower tariff, but of what is called the exemption du surtax d'entrepbt, must sail directly from Canada to France.

maintopic: OCEAN STEAMSHIP SUBSIDIES.
speechtext: As I understand, there is a subsidy from the government of France.

maintopic: OCEAN STEAMSHIP SUBSIDIES.
speechtext:
Yes, of a similar amount.
Bill reported, read the third time, and passed.

maintopic: THE PACIFIC CABLE.

speechtext: Bill (No. 45) to amend the Pacific Cable Act, 1S99-the Prime Minister (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier) read the second time, and House went into committee thereon.

maintopic: THE PACIFIC CABLE.
THE PACIFIC CABLE.
speechtext: Since the statement made by the Postmaster General, have there been any further negotiations made with reference to this matter ?

maintopic: THE PACIFIC CABLE.
speechtext:
Yes, we have been engaged in correspondence upon a certain action taken by the government of New South Wales. The government of New South Wales, since entering confederation, has made arrangements with the Eastern Cable Company by which it gives them their business. We have been protesting against that arrangement, and the correspondence is still going on. I may say that we have consulted our law officers of the Crown upon the subject of that arrangement, and according to their interpretation the arrangement would be very detrimental to our interests. The law officers of the Imperial government, however, dissent from the view taken by our officers. Correspondence is still going on. I am not clear whether our officers are right in looking upon the arrangement as detrimental to the project so far as it concerns us. However, I shall move this clause, to cover contingencies :
This Act shall only come into operation on proclamation made by the Governor General in Council.
Because we want to see the end of this correspondence before this Act comes into operation.

maintopic: THE PACIFIC CABLE.
speechtext:
When this subject was up before it was suggested that a provision ought to be made, by the insertion of a penalty in the contract, for the due performance of the work. The Postmaster General was not then in a position to tell the
House whether such a penalty clause existed in the contract. I think it is very important that such a clause should be inserted, because the firm or company which has undertaken to construct this cable is owned and controlled by the great cable company that has objected so much to the construction of this cable. I hope there will be a provision in the contract insisting on a certain time limit for the performance of the contract, and a penalty if'it is not carried out.
On section 2,

maintopic: THE PACIFIC CABLE.
speechtext: Does the right hon. gentleman see any public reason why the opinion that was given by our own law officers in reference to the point which he mentioned, and the opinion given by the law officers of the Crown in England, should not be laid on the Table ?

maintopic: THE PACIFIC CABLE.
speechtext:
I see no public reason why they should not be laid upon the Table. I will take a note of it and bring down the papers.
Bill, as amended, reported, read the third time, and passed. *

maintopic: SL'PPLY-THE BELL TELEPHONE COMPANY.

speechtext: The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Hon. W. S. Fielding;) moved that the House go again into Committee of Supply.

maintopic: SL'PPLY-THE BELL TELEPHONE COMPANY.
speechtext:
Before you leave the Chair, I desire to direct the attention of the Prime Minister to a Bill among the Public Bills and Orders. That Bill (No. 101) has for its object to make clear certain legislation which was passed by the parliament of Canada in 1892, respecting the Bell Telephone Company of Canada. I may say in passing that this Bill was read the first time on the 28th of March last, nearly two months ago, but an opportunity has not since been given to proceed with it. and therefore I make a request that the Prime Minister will take this Bill off its position on the Order paper and have it passed before the session closes.
As I have already stated, the intention of the Bill is to make clear what seems to be a defect in the legislation of 1892 respecting the Bell Telephone Company. In that year the company asked for and obtained the permission of parliament to increase its capital from $2,000,000 to $5,000,000. But, parliament, in its wisdom, placed a restriction upon the powers of the company which had not theretofore existed, the restriction being that the existing rates should not be increased without the consent of the Governor in Council. The Bill presented to parliament by the Bell Telephone Company was in charge of the Hon. R. W. Scott, when it was "passing through the Senate. There are

just two references which 1 desire the permission of the House to make ; one as to the power which was given to the company when it was incorporated in 1S80, and the other, as to the reasons by which parliament was moved to place some restriction upon that power. At page 196 of the Senate ' Hansard ' of 1892, 1 find reference made by Hon. Mr. Power to the extraordinary power that the company obtained when it was chartered in 1880. Mr. Power said :
That at the time that Act of the Bell Telephone Company was passed, parliament was not as careful In safeguarding the public interests in cities and towns as they should have been, is a matter of great consequence. As a matter of fact, by increasing the capital of this company to almost this indefinite extent, we give them the right for an unlimited time to go on exercising in municipalities throughout Canada their extraordinary powers to deal with the public highways-powers which should be restricted.
The Standing Committee on Railways, Telegraphs and Harbours of the Senate, in reporting the Bill with this restrictive clause, spoke, through its chairman, the Hon. Mr. Dickey, as follows :
With regard to the amendment, referring to the rates, it is not a clause which places the rates entirely under the control of the Governor in Council, but it is a clause, which, after the rates were explained to us, was introduced to limit the power of the company to charge those rates in the direction of an increase without the consent of the Governor in Council, so as to afford a protection, as far as we could, to the public, that no exorbitant rates would be the result of this increased capital, and the wording of the clause shows that the rates charged are not hereafter to be increased without the consent of the Governor in Council.
The Hon. Mr. Scott added :
The chairman of the committee has explained fully the purport of the amendments, and the House thoroughly understands and will probably approve of them.
.	.	.	. The House understands the subject now.
The Bill was passed practically unanimously, with this restrictive clause in it. I do not think there is a record of a division. In 1897, the company applied to the Governor in Council for permission to increase its rates. The application for permission to increase the rates was stoutly resisted by many municipalities in the Dominion of Canada, and delegations representing these municipalities appeared before the committee in opposition to the application of the company. No action has been taken upon that application, although, I believe, many communications have passed between the municipalities and the Governor in Council, urging that a decision should be made. On .Tuly 24, 1900, in reply to an inquiry from the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals, an opinion"was given by the hon. Minister of Justice with respect to the efficacy of the legislation of 1892, which is as follows : Mr. CLARKE.
Ottawa, July 24, 1900.
My dear Mr. Blair,-I beg to acknowledge receipt of your letter of the 9th instant, and of Mr. Caswell's letter, inclosed therewith, in relation to the rents charged by the Bell Telephone Co.
In reply to your letter, I may state that I am strongly of opinion that the clause in the Act of 1892, providing that the existing rates shall not be increased without the consent of the Governor in Council, is legally ineffective so far as subscribers are concerned, and that proceedings to restrain the company from increasing the rents charged to subscribers would be unsuccessful. For that reason, I think the government might decline to take proceedings, even if otherwise it would be its duty to thus intervene for the protection of the subscribers. But, in my opinion, it would not in any case be incumbent upon the government to take the initiative in any such proceedings. If any person, aggrieved by the action of the company, desires upon his own responsibility to apply to the courts, and is advised that he should do so in the name of the Attorney General of the Dominion, the question whether he should be permitted to do so would be considered upon a proper application being made to the Department of Justice, for leave to take such proceedings.
Yours faithfully,
(Signed) DAVID MILLS.
Now, Mr. Speaker, in view of this opinion of the bon. Minister of Justice, and in view of the continued violation of the provisions of the Act of 1892, this Bill, to which I have referred, No. 101 on the Order paper, has been introduced for the purpose of making clear what the intention of the Act of 1892 was. The company has ignored in many instances the obligations which parliament has imposed upon it.

maintopic: SL'PPLY-THE BELL TELEPHONE COMPANY.
speechtext:
I would say to the hon. gentleman (Mr. Clarke) that on the motion to go into Committee of Supply, we may discuss almost any question, but it is specially provided in our parliamentary procedure, that we have no right to discuss a question that is on the Order paper. If we look at Bourinot, page 548, we will see this :
A great latitude being always allowed on such occasions ; but they may not refer specifically to any vote which has passed, or is about to be
discussed in committee	nor to any
Bill or order of the day.
The question that the hon. gentleman is discussing relates to a Bill which is on the Order paper, and I would call his attention to this fact.

maintopic: SL'PPLY-THE BELL TELEPHONE COMPANY.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have no '[DOT]desire to violate the rules of the House, and I will confine my remarks to asking the right hon. Prime Minister to introduce legislation that will make effective the legislation of 1892. I do not desire to take up the time of the House, but, I might quote many cases for the information of the right hon. gentleman of flagrant violations of the law which have been committed by the company. In the adjoining Chamber, the company asked for permission to increase its capital

to $10,000,000, to double the capital which was authorized in 1892. The other Chamber, in its wisdom, declined to accept the report of the Committee on Banking and Commerce, and the Bill has been withdrawn. There will be no opportunity for a private member to promote legislation having the object in view that I desire to see accomplished, and it is in the public interest that until a general Act has been passed which will limit the powers of such a monopoly as the Bell Telephone Company, some attempt should be made before parliament closes to make effective what has been declared to be defective in the legislation of 1892. 1 do not know whether I have made myself clear or not. My desire to be as brief as possible is the reason why I am curtailing my remarks, but it is not an unreasonable request that I make of the right lion, gentleman. I think it is a most reasonable one. It will give the government an opportunity during the recess to prepare a Bill which will be in the public interest, which will govern the rates to be charged by the Bell Telephone Company, and by similar companies doing business in the Dominion of Canada. In view of the extraordinary powers which that company has been given by the parliament of Canada, powers which have been given, I believe, to no other company by this parliament, amongst them the power to go into a municipality and occupy the streets of that municipality without the consent of the municipality, it is not an unreasonable request that if these powers are to be continued to the company, somebody should be named by parliament that shall have control over the rates to be charged by the company in the cities and towns where it is permitted to exercise this authority.
There is no reason why such action should not be taken. The company is in its very nature a monopoly. To give an efficient telephone service in a city or town, it must be done by one company, which therefore has a monopoly ; and that being the case it is surely the duty of the legislative body which vested such enormous powers in this company, to, see that these powers shall not be abused, but that the rights of the public shall be protected. For this reason I have taken the liberty, at this late period of the session-and because the company's Bill was withdrawn only the day before yesterday in the Senate-to ask the Prime Minister if he will not introduce a Bill similar to Bill No. 101, which will, until a general Act has been passed, give effect to what was the intention of parliament under its legislation in 1882. when power was given to the Bell Telephone Company to increase its capital from $2,000,000 to $5,000,000.

maintopic: SL'PPLY-THE BELL TELEPHONE COMPANY.
speechtext:
Even if my hon. friend (Mr. Clarke) could, according to the rules of the House, move his Bill now, I doubt very much if the House would
pass it. The object of the Bill is to amend, not 51 public Act but a private Act, and I doubt very much if the House will undertake to do that. A private Act confers certain franchises and advantages on a certain body oi; individuals. This is done under certain rules of parliament which have been adopted for the protection of private interests. I do not believe that the House could legally proceed to amend a private Act by a public Act. Even if parliament should exercise that power-disregarding all the rules that have been made for the protection of private Bills-I am quite sure that parliament would not do so unless ample notice were given to the parties interested so that they could be heard, and could present what objections they might have against such legislation. At this late period of the session, even if parliament had the power to pass this Bill in the form in which the hon. member (Mr. Clarke) is introducing it, parliament would not, I believe, interfere with the private legislation of the Bell Telephone Company without giving that company an opportunity to be heard. My hon. friend (Mr. Clarke) will agree with me, I think, that it would not be competent for parliament to deal with this question at this period of the session.

maintopic: SL'PPLY-THE BELL TELEPHONE COMPANY.
speechtext: I would remind the right hon. gentleman, that the company has been made aware of the fact that this Bill is before parliament, because it was presented in the Senate committee as an amendment to the Bell Telephone Bill, and it has been discussed in that branch of the legislature for nearly a month.

maintopic: SL'PPLY-THE BELL TELEPHONE COMPANY.
speechtext: That is not notice that this Bill would be taken up in this House. I am not aware that the company has received any notice of that kind.

maintopic: SL'PPLY-THE BELL TELEPHONE COMPANY.
speechtext:
I think I can suggest a way by which the right hon. gentleman can legislate on this matter at this present time. I have been looking up this question recently, and I was surprised to find two things. First, in 1882 a very peculiar Bill was put through this House presumably in the public interest, but which now turns out to be solely in the interests of the Bell Telephone company. I have also discovered that the Bill which was introduced in 1892 turns out to be inoperative. It would seem that some design was resorted to and succeeded, to get ahead of the public and to use parliament to improve the position of the Bell Telephone Company. In 18S2, there was passed a Bill which declared that a ' telephone ' was not a ' telegraph,' and an easy way out of the present difficulty is for this parliament to repeal that Act and so bring the telephone companies under the telegraph Act and regulations. The Act of 1882 was passed presumedly in the interest of the province of Prince Edward Island. There is a telegraph monopoly in Prince Edward

Island, and a little Bill was introduced here, I declaring that a ' telephone ' was not a ' telegraph ' in order to enable the people of Prince Edward Island to have telephones. A very significant debate toook place in this House on that occasion, some brief extracts from which I shall reaS :

maintopic: THE WORD TELEGRAPH.

speechtext:
Sir HECTOR LANGEVIN moved the second reading of Bill (No. 166) declaratory of the meaning of the word Telegraph in certain cases.
Bill read the second time ; and House resolved itself into Committee.
(In the Committee.)

maintopic: THE WORD TELEGRAPH.
speechtext: I think we require some explanation of this Bill. It appears to me that it may affect very important private interests.

maintopic: THE WORD TELEGRAPH.
speechtext:
The object of this Bill is simply to declare that the telephone is not a telegraph. The Anglo-American Telegraph Co., which has a telegraph line in Prince Edward Island, will not allow any telephone to be erected on the island without receiving tribute therefor ; and as the Telegraph Company, under its charter, has exclusive power to build telegraph lines on the island, and as the telephone was not known then or discovered, they will not allow any telephones to be established there without paying tribute to them. This seems to be an extension of their powers, and this Bill is brought forward for the purpose of allowing telephone companies to establish telephones there as well as elsewhere by simply stating that telephones are not telegraphs.
It was a very innocent looking measure, and I believe Sir Hector Langevin then thought this was the only object of the Bill. But listen to what Mr. Blake said immediately after, and it is prophetic of the condition of affairs that exists to-day :

maintopic: THE WORD TELEGRAPH.
speechtext:
But for this Bill telephones would be telegraphs-and I believe it has been so decided in the English courts of justice in cases in which it was contended that the creating of telephonic arrangements was an infringement upon the exclusive rights of the Crown to the telegraphs. It may be that by this wide measure of legislation we are giving rights to be assumed by patentees of telephonic rights, which do not exist under the law ; it may that we are creating monopolies even more extensive than that which the hon. gentleman says exist on the island by the telephone and telegraph being held to be identical. I should prefer very much, at this late stage of the session, unless there is some necessity for it, that some more limited measure of legislation might be devised which would not be so likely to produce such far-reaching consequences as might arise from this Bill.
Further on, Mr. Blake said :

maintopic: THE WORD TELEGRAPH.
speechtext:
I do not know how that was done. It is not from that aspect of the question that I am discussing the Bill ; I was much more interested in the other aspect and which deserves our most serious consideration. If it be the case that under the Englsh decision telephone is included in telegraph, and if it does follow from that

because these telephonic arrangements were all patented in England-that there is an exclusive right to the patentee, it may to the greatest possible advantage to the Mr. MACLEAN.
telephonic proprietors, and if the proposition to create a legislative distinction which does not now exist between the telegraph and the telephone, and if it be useful to create that distinction for the purpose of permitting telephones to be erected in Prince Edward Island, can not some declaration be made in the Bill that this definition is not to confer on the patentee of the telephone any other or greater rights than they might possess but for that, so as to preserve the interests of the public in not creating a right which would be created by the opposition of this law, so as to give an interpretation to the word telegraph different from that which according to right and justice does not belong to it. It is very important we should not step hastily in this matter.
There was a further discussion, and the Hon. David Mills, the present Minister of Justice took part in it, and here is what he said :

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the Senate
maintopic: THE WORD TELEGRAPH.
speechtext: When I dissented from the hon. member for Victoria, I did so from the recollection of the decision of the English judge, I think it was Justice Stephens who was the presiding judge, and who gave an elaborate judgment after men of high scientific attainments were examined, and after learned counsel were heard, to the effect that not merely upon the provisions of the statute, but also from the nature of the two inventions that a telephone was a telegraph, and the control of the telephone in England was upon their scientific identity.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the Senate
maintopic: THE WORD TELEGRAPH.
speechtext:
I beg to move :
That the Bill be not now read a third time, but referred back to the committee with instructions to amend it by adding to the end of the second clause the following words :	" Or any
right now existing.' "
Both Mr. Blake and Mr. Mills saw that in taking the word ' telephone ' and not associating it with the same idea as ' telegraph.' the public interests would be jeopardized. They have been jeopardized now, and the way to correct the evil is to repeal that general Act which made the telephone and telegraph dissimilar terms. If we do that, this telephone company will come under the general law regulating telegraphs, which would be much more in the interest of the public than the present state of affairs. The present Minister of Justice, knowing wliat took place, and having declared that this private Act is inoperative so far'as the public interests are concerned, the government would be justified in the public interest in repealing that Act of 1882. It is a very peculiar thing that two Acts have gone through this parliament which have turned out to be for the express benefit of the Bell Telephone Company and against the public interest; and the proposal of this session, as it was presented to parliament, was to free that great monopoly from all control of its rates by parliament or the government. This should not be allowed. It is one of the most enormous scandals in Canada to-day that the Bell Telephone Company, controlling a great public convenience, should not be subject to government regulation. The easiest way to bring it under government regulation is

to repeal that Act and put it in the same position as telegraph companies ; and in the meantime, if it is shown that the public are injured, is it not the duty of the government to see that this parliament corrects that injury at once ? I know that the Prime Minister is going to say that he is not in favour of corrective legislation. But I am. There is no legislation so good as corrective legislation in the public interest ; and it would be quite in order, after all the discussion which has taken place, and no injury to the Bell Telephone Company, for the government to make the measure introduced by the hon. member for West Toronto a government measure, so as to give the public the protection they desire. Of course, the easy way out of all these difficulties is to nationalize the telegraph and telephone services of this country, and we have heard so much about that that probably we shall have a Bill along that line next session. The right hon. leader of the government bows his head, whatever that means. But in the meantime he would make no mistake if he made the measure of the hon. member for West Toronto a government measure, and put it through the House, and repealed that Act which declared that a telephone was not a telegraph. The other day the government did this in the ease of a private Bill- the Manitoba Railway Bill-and they could do the same thing in this instance without doing any substantial injury to the Bell Telephone Company ; because that company introduced a Bill into parliament themselves, and if they chose to withdraw it from another Chamber, there is no reason why we should not go on and pass a Bill, of which they received ample notice, which has been on the Order paper for weeks, and which I believe would pass this House ; and it ought to be done because of the two measures which have 'already been passed through this parliament, I believe surreptitiously, to the great advantage of the Bell Telephone Company, and to the detriment of the public interest.

maintopic: THE WORD TELEGRAPH.
speechtext:
McCarthy (North Simcoe). Whatever little power or influence I have is entirely in accord with the hon. member for West Toronto. We have a measure of control over railway rates and other rates, and it seems to me that the parliament of Canada ought likewise to have control over telephone rates. There may be a great deal said on behalf of the telephone company. In another Chamber of this parliament a great deal has been said pro and con in regard to what the rates should be. We have not that question before us at the present time, and I do not propose to discuss it. But I do think that some equitable basis should be established whereby the company will be protected and the public will be protected ; and in that way a great deal of friction and useless discussion in this House and in the country would be obviated. We who come from the city of Toronto are charged with being prejudiced and with wanting too much ; but I speak with some personal knowledge, and I say without fear of contradiction, that there is in that city discrimination in rates, one person paying $25 for a house telephone, and another person paying $35. There may be some explanation of that, but to the ordinary logical mind it does not appear that there can be a satisfactory explanation. If we had a tariff of rates which had to be submitted to the Governor in Council or in some way made subject to the control of parliament, that difficulty would be obviated.
Mi-. N. A. BELCOURT (Ottawa). I am not prepared to disagree with what has been said by previous speakers as to what legislation we should adopt to protect the public ; but lest the House might be under a misapprehension as to the Bill which has been introduced, I wish to say a few words. I want to correct a mistake made by the hon. member for East York when he says that the company has had full notice, and that this House might well go on now and discuss a Bill of this sort, because the company introduced a Bill itself. The facts of the case are these. The Bell Telephone Company introduced a Bill for an increase of its capital from $5,000,000 to $10,000,000. and nothing more. Somebody in the Upper House moved that the section in the Act of 1S92 which said that the rates could not be increased except with the consent of the Governor in Council, should be eximnged. and a more restrictive clause inserted. It is quite clear that the restrictive legislation sought to be imposed upon the company came upon them unawares, and that they would not be in a position to discuss the Bill of the hon. gentleman from Toronto West. It seems to me that this is largely a dispute between the city of Toronto and the Bell Telephone Company. Notwithstanding the efforts of the city of Toronto to enlist the sympathies of other municipalities throughout Canada, I do not think any other protest has been made against the manner in. which the company has administered its affairs throughout Canada. I am not a special advocate in any way of the Bell Telephone Company, and I do think, at least I hope that the hon. gentleman who proposes this Bill desires to do the company no injustice ; but I must say. in justice to the company, that in the city of Ottawa we have had a magnificent service. The Bell Telephone Company have not ground the people down, as the representatives of the city of Toronto have declared.

maintopic: THE WORD TELEGRAPH.
speechtext: Might I remind the hon. gentleman that representatives of the Ottawa Board of Trade appeared to support the position taken by those who opposed the increase of the capital stock of the company unless this restrictive provision was made ?

maintopic: THE WORD TELEGRAPH.
speechtext: I cannot say whether they did or not, though I know they appeared. But what I say is that this appears to be largely a fight between the city of Toronto and the Bell Telephone company. If it is nothing of the kind, I would like to ask the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Clarke) why he did not make his Bill applicable to all telephone companies in Canada ?

maintopic: THE WORD TELEGRAPH.
speechtext: As I am advised, parliament has never given any other telephone company the extraordinary powers and privileges which were given the Bell Telephone Company. When that companv came to parliament in 1S92 to get authority to increase its capital from $2,000,000 to $5,000,000, parliament then passed legislation giving control over the rates to the Governor General in Council. And it is because that Act was found inoperative that we ask by the proposed legislation to make it operative and effective. The company accepted the legislation of 1S92. It recognized the validity of that legislation by going to the Governor General in Council in 1897 with a schedule of rates, increasing the rates all over the Dominion ; and it is because the Act giving control to the Governor in Council has been declared inoperative, that I ask for further legislation.

maintopic: THE WORD TELEGRAPH.
speechtext: I think the House will agree with me that if the hon. gentleman did not want to create the impression that this was a war between the city of Toronto and the Bell Telephone Company, he would have done better to have introduced a general law applicable to all telephone companies. In the province of Quebec there are at least fifty or sixty telephone companies doing business, against which there is no such restriction.

maintopic: THE WORD TELEGRAPH.
speechtext: Have they the same powers as the Bell Telephone Company of going into municipalities without their consent ?

maintopic: THE WORD TELEGRAPH.
speechtext: They have the powers that were conferred by provincial legislature on the Bell Telephone Company. There is no restriction on their rates and that is the question now before the House. If my hon. friends had proposed a Bill applicable to all telephone companies, there might be no objection. I believe that in the interests of the public generally, telephone companies might be subject to some control, but it does seem unjust to the Bell Telephone Company, which after all is deserving of some credit, that it should be singled out and made the subject of all the attacks of hon. gentlemen from Toronto. It is because the Bell Company, which has done a great deal for Canada, is unjustly dealt with in being thus singled out, that I protest. It may be that the telephone system has come into such general use and is of such utility to the general public and partakes so much of the character of a monopoly that the gov-

maintopic: THE WORD TELEGRAPH.
speechtext: eminent might well consider the nationalization of the system. I am not prepared to express an opinion one way or the other on that point, but in the name of all those who desire fair-play and justice, I protest against these unwarranted attacks. I do not know anything of Toronto-

maintopic: THE WORD TELEGRAPH.
speechtext: You speak as if you knew a great deal.

maintopic: THE WORD TELEGRAPH.
speechtext: But I do not think parliament should legislate for Toronto only. The hon. gentleman by his Bill is asking us to interpret a private agreement.

maintopic: THE WORD TELEGRAPH.
speechtext: The hon. member has no right at this stage to discuss the merits of the Bill.

maintopic: THE WORD TELEGRAPH.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman said he protested in the name of-and then he paused. I would like to know in whose name. Is it in the name of his constituents of the city of Ottawa ? No, but in the name of the Bell Telephone Company. His speech from start to finish was simply a defence of that company. He sets that company up as a martyr, because the Bill proposed by the hon. member for Toronto West does not apply to the fifty or sixty little telephone companies down in the province of Quebec, that have either wires or appliances of their own and have but a very small tariff, if any at all. We have here a company which is encompassing the whole country and asking powers from the parliament of Canada to have unlimited power in this Dominion to crush out every other opposing telephone company. They propose to increase their capital from $5,000,000 to $10,-000,000-a very innocent looking proposal. What do they want with $10,000,000 ? To string up a few poles throughout the country and put their appliances into households.

maintopic: THE WORD TELEGRAPH.
speechtext: I rise to a point of order. The hon. gentleman is discussing the merits of the Bill.

maintopic: THE WORD TELEGRAPH.
speechtext: I have already pointed 'ofit the rule, that on a motion to go into supply, you must not discuss the merits of a Bill which is not before the House.

maintopic: THE WORD TELEGRAPH.
speechtext: I am discussing the broad and general principle upon which the Bill is founded. I say that there is no justification.

maintopic: THE WORD TELEGRAPH.
speechtext: Order.

maintopic: THE WORD TELEGRAPH.
speechtext: The hon. member has no right to discuss the general principle on which the Bill is founded.

maintopic: THE WORD TELEGRAPH.
speechtext: I have the Bill here. I was speaking

maintopic: THE WORD TELEGRAPH.
speechtext: Order.

maintopic: THE WORD TELEGRAPH.
speechtext:
I am discussing the point of order. There is nothing in the Bill we have before us about increasing the capital stock from $5,000,000 to $10,000,000.

It was that that I was discussing, and let me say that if this company are not quite doubling their rates they are increasing them more than 00 per cent out in the rural districts. We used to have a rate of say 15 cents from Woodbridge to Toronto.

maintopic: THE WORD TELEGRAPH.
speechtext: I rise to a point of order.

maintopic: THE WORD TELEGRAPH.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman is raising the same point as before.

maintopic: THE WORD TELEGRAPH.
speechtext: Yes, and I hope that the hon. gentleman will submit to your ruling, Mr. Speaker.

maintopic: THE WORD TELEGRAPH.
speechtext: What is the point?

maintopic: THE WORD TELEGRAPH.
speechtext: The point is that the hon. gentleman is discussing a Bill which is on the Order paper, and is not now before the House

maintopic: THE WORD TELEGRAPH.
speechtext:
He is doing nothing of the kind.
Mr. BELCOURT-and which cannot possibly come up for discussion.

maintopic: THE WORD TELEGRAPH.
speechtext: I was not discussing anything of the kind. The hon. gentleman himself wandered from Dan to Beersheba. [DOT]He did not comply with the rules of the House and was very properly called to order.

maintopic: THE WORD TELEGRAPH.
speechtext: And I took my seat.

maintopic: THE WORD TELEGRAPH.
speechtext: The hon. member for Ottawa is sure to be found on the side of the monopolies whenever there is a conflict between them and the people.

maintopic: THE WORD TELEGRAPH.
speechtext: The point of order has been raised by the hon. member for Ottawa that we have no right to discuss now the merits of the Bill of the hon. member for West Toronto. The Bill, if I understood what was said, has to do with the rates which the Bell Telephone Company are charging, and I would ask hon. members not to discuss the merits of that Bill on the motion to go into supply.

maintopic: THE WORD TELEGRAPH.
speechtext:
I was purposely avoiding discussing the substance of the Bill. The first clause refers to the obligation to furnish telephones, and the second provides that no higher rates than those in force shall be charged. I shall avoid both of these, and so shall not leave myself open to the charge of discussing the Bill. My hon. friend from Ottawa (Mr. Belcourt) says that there are fifty or sixty telephone companies in the province of Quebec, and that there is no proposal to apply rules regulating rates to them. The reason is, that the Bell Telephone Company has proved itself a grasping. greedy corporation. This is not an affair of the city of Toronto only, but of every city, town and village in Canada. 1 applied for a telephone service, and though
there was a telephone wire going past my door, I was refused a service at auy price.

maintopic: THE WORD TELEGRAPH.
speechtext: What was the reason given ?

maintopic: THE WORD TELEGRAPH.
speechtext:
That there must be five telephones. There is a telephone ottiee at Woodbridge, and we wanted a telephone. They said : You must get five. 1 said : We do not want five, but we will pay for two. That was refused, and we are without a telephone to-day. These people are not considering the public convenience, they have a monopoly, and they think only of their own affairs. They have what must necessarily be a monopoly, and they are using their power to the detriment of the best interests of the country. They should be held to strict account. If we give them what must be the exclusive control-for there cannot be competition in these matters-the parliament of Canada must lay down the rules and conditions to govern the business, rules that shall be fair to the people and fair to the company. Why, they want the sole control in Canada. But, I can tell them, and their agent in this House, that they are not going to have it from the parliament of Canada, that the people will be heard, and that public opinion will prevent the Bell Telephone Company from keeping the unchecked monopoly which they have now, and which they wish to have still further extended.

maintopic: MONTREAL AND SOUTHERN COUNTIES RAILWAY.

speechtext: House in committee on Bill (No. 112) respecting the Montreal and Southern Counties Railway Company.-Mr. Carroll.

maintopic: MONTREAL AND SOUTHERN COUNTIES RAILWAY.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I would like to call the attention of the committee to a point of order in connection with this Bill. The title is ' An Act respecting the Montreal and Southern Counties Railway Company.' As chairman of the Committee on Standing Orders, it becomes my duty and the duty of that committee, under rule 63 of the House, to see that every private Bill and every petition asking for leave to introduce a Bill corresponds with the notice required by law. Of course, incidentally, It is the duty not only of that committee, but of any hon. member of the House at any time that a Bill appears to transcend the notice and the petition that the House accepted to call the attention of the House to the fact, and ask the House to take such action as may seem proper in the premises. In this Bill powers are asked for not contemplated in the notice or the petition, as Is quite apparent, not exactly on the face of the Bill, but on the face of the Bill as compared with the notice or the petition. I have in my hand the petition which passed through the Standing Orders Committee and was recommended to the House, as well as a copy of the notices. I cannot say just here that any reflection can be cast upon the officers of the Standing Orders Committee, because they ascertained that the notice and the petition corresponded, and this Bill started upon its passage through the various stages all right, but now, when the Bill itself comes to be considered, wre find that it has introduced in it powers and requirements not at all contemplated in the notice. When I state, without at all arguing the merits of this Bill, that it provides for the construction of a railway around seven or eight different counties in the province of Quebec, in a very ill-defined manner, of course, we see that the necessity of giving notice that these powers are to be applied for, is of very great importance, because, otherwise, the Bill might pass through its various stages without the attention of the persons interested in it being called to the fact. The notice was published properly and in due time that:
The Montreal Southern Counties Railway Company will apply to the parliament of Canada at the present session for an Act extending the delay fixed for the construction of the railway.
That is one thing that they asked for. Second :

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: MONTREAL AND SOUTHERN COUNTIES RAILWAY.
speechtext:
Granting it the power to connect with other railways.
That is another thing.
Making arrangements for the use of other railway lines, to construct, maintain and operate vessels and power vehicles, elevators, warehouses, docks, wharfs and other buildings and powers to dispose of same ; and all other necessary powers.
Powers necessary and incidental to these powers asked for. If the Bill, when it came to the cognizance of hon. members, had complied with the notice on these points, of course, this point of order could not properly be taken. But what do we find in the Bill ? We find in the first place that the first section asks that the railway be made a steam railway. The charter of the Montreal and Southern Counties Railway Company, which was given in
1897,	was an Act for the construction of an electric railway. That Act was amended in
1898,	when application was made for certain other privileges, applicable to an electric railway, and we are right in assuming that the public were not opposed to the granting of these privileges. I may add here that the time for the construction of the road had absolutely expired and the terms of the notice asked for an extension of time, although the terms of the notice were unintentionally slightly misleading, because they should have asked for a revival of the Act. The time had absolutely expired, not a stroke had been done on the road, but perhaps it may be construed that asking for an extension of the delay virtually is a request to revive the charter. But, a clause making it a steam railway completely changes the whole situation, and in my view, completely nullifies the value of the notice, the value of the petition based upon the notice and the consent given by the Standing Orders Committee that this Bill should be introduced to the House. If we pass this Bill we shall change this road from an electric to a steam railway, placing it under the Railway Act, with all the powers and responsibilities of a steam road, something that the parties interested in the seven or eight counties certainly never had ample notice of. They have in a fashion appeared and asked that some consideration be given to their wishes. The only place in which the views of the opponents of a steam railway can be heard is in the Railway Committee, where a hearing can be granted, where all the points can be made and all the data presented. Some hon. gentlemen may ask : Why was this matter not noticed before ? 'I may say that this Bill came up in the Railway Committee in due course, at the close of last Friday, after a keenly contested Bill had been fought over with considerable interest. This Bill was taken up as the last business of the meeting, when a large number of the members of the committee bad left and this change was not noticed.

Not only lias the change from an electric road to a steam road been inserted in the Bill after the Standing Orders Committee had approved of the additional notice, but they ask for power to bridge the River St. Lawrence, which is not contained in the original legislation, and is not contained either in the notice or in the petition. Section 2 is so intermingled with the section of the Act that I will not read it; however, the meaning is that it also extends the bonding powers of the company to $20,000 a mile for each mile of single track. I do not intend to enter into the merits of the Bill except to call attention to these three important changes between the notice and petition and the Bill itself, and to ask the intervention of the chairman of the committee to have it referred back in due course to the Committee on Standing Orders, in order that a third report on these points may be made to the House.. I will read the rules of the House which have been laid down in previous proceedings, as they are found in Sir John Bourinot's work on parliamentary procedure:
In case the committee do not so report, and a member is of opinion that certain provisions of a Bill are not contemplated in the notice for the same, he may raise a point of order, and it will be for the Speaker to decide. In the case of a Bill to amend the Acts incorporating the Great Western Railway Company, it was decided that the Bill should be referred to the Committee on Standing Orders to report as to the matter in doubt. That committee subsequently reported favourably on the Bill. In such a case it is the more regular course to discharge the order for consideration in Committee of the Whole, and then refer the Bill to the Committee on Standing Orders.	[DOT]
I need not read the report of the debate that took place on that occasion, but I will read an entry in the Journals of the House of 1870, which, I think, should guide the committee to some extent :
The Order of the Day being read, for the second reading of the Bill to amend the Acts of incorporation of the Great Western Railway Company ;
The Hon. Mr. Carling moved, seconded by Mr. Shanly, and the question being proposed, that the Bill be now read a second time ;
And objection being taken by Mr. Cameron, member for the electoral district of the south riding of the county of Huron, that certain of the provisions of the said Bill, as amended by the Select Standing Committee on Railways, Canals and Telegraph Lines, were not contemplated in the notice given under the rules of the House, nor in the petition praying for the passing of the said Bill ;
Mr. Speaker decided, that the Bill should be referred to the Select Standing Committee on Standing Orders to report whether the powers to be conferred are in excess of the notice given, or whether they are substantially included in it.
That is all I can ask just now. It may be said that this is not the time to raise a question of order, and there may be some reason for that contention, but if it should be held by the Chair that this is not the 170
time for raising the question in that way, I will give notice of a resolution which will effect the same object. I will move that the Bill be referred back to the Standing Orders Committee for further consideration, and to find whether the powers to be conferred are in excess of the notice given and of the petition. For the present, I will leave this question in the hands of the committee.

maintopic: MONTREAL AND SOUTHERN COUNTIES RAILWAY.
speechtext: I do not think the point is well taken by my hon. friend from Yarmouth (Mr. Flint). His Bill has passed the Standing Orders Committee twice. It has passed the Standing Orders Committee of this House, and I am informed it has also passed the Standing Orders Committee of the Senate. More than that, it has passed the Railway Committee and been discussed there. Now, this Bill is a very important one, and much interest is taken in it by the people of Montreal, and the people residing in the adjoining counties. My hon. friend contends that the notices do not cover the object of the Bill. I have the notices here, and I see by them that the promoters ask parliament to give some connecting lines to the projected railway. Well, it happens that this road is to be operated by electricity, but the connections which are asked by the Bill happen to be railway connections which are operated by steam. Therefore, the notices imply that they will have to operate by steam when the electric railway will connect with such railways. I must say at once that when the Bill first came before parliament some two or three years ago, the originators did not ask that the words ' except by steam power ' should be inserted in the Bill. That was imposed upon them by some of their opponents. Now, I must say, speaking for the promoters, that if they are restricted to the use of electricity, the Bill will be of no use to them, because they cannot make connections that will enable them to reach Montreal, which is the principal objective point. Therefore, I think that the question raised by my hon. friend is not well taken, especially in view of the fact that the Bill has already passed the Standing Orders Committee of this House and of the Senate, and also the Railway Committee.

(Translation.) Mr. Chairman, I am surprised at the opposition offered to a Bill



which concerns only a small section of the province of Quebec, and I am still more astonished that objection should be taken to this measure by my hon. freud (Mr. Flynn) who comes from the maritime provinces. speechtext: House in committee on Bill (No. 88) to amend the Canadian Nurses Association.- Mr. Clarke.
