speechtext:
There would appear to be some reasons why this Mr. DEMERS (St. John & Iberville).
Bill should not pass at this particular time. The Bill has been before the committee on more than one occasion, and it seems to me that the information we have so far received does not justify its passage. It may be that there is some information which the committee was not put in possession of, and if so I would be glad to have it from the hon. gentleman in charge of the Bill. My opposition to the Bill is not very strong I am bound to say, and for my part I will withdraw opposition if the hon. gentleman (Mr. Clarke) can show to the House that there is a demand; any general demand for this measure.

maintopic: CANADIAN NURSES ASSOCIATION.
speechtext: This Bill is very similar in many respects to a Bill which was introduced in the House twelve months ago, and was withdrawn because objection was taken to it by some hon. members. It is introduced again, with the features that were objected to last year completely eliminated. It has been before the House for nearly two months. It was reported by the Miscellaneous Private Bills Committee a couple of weeks ago, was referred back by the House, has been reconsidered by the committee and reported again. The fact that ladies occupying a most prominent position in the profession of nursing, from one end of the Dominion to the other, are seeking this incorporation, is, I take it, an evidence that there is a necessity for an organization of this kind. Similar institutions are in existence in the United States, and in the mother country, and because of the non-existence of such an association in Canada, our nurses do not occupy the position which their ability and experience entitle them to occupy. I do not know what information the hon. gentleman (Mr. Johnston, Cape Breton) requires, but if there is any particular clause in the Bill to which he objects, I shall be glad to give him information respecting it.

maintopic: CANADIAN NURSES ASSOCIATION.
speechtext: I do not think for one moment that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Clarke) would introduce a measure of this kind, if representations -were not made to him that it was desirable, by persons engaged in this very important profession throughout the country. This Act will to a large extent affect persons in his constituency in Toronto as well as in other large cities, but I would remind him that it also effects the rest of the Dominion. So far as I have been able to ascertain, certain parts of Canada have not been consulted about this Bill. I have not been able to ascertain whether those interested in Nova Scotia have been consulted, and if so. and if they endorse it, I am perfectly satisfied that the Bill should pass. As the Bill affects a large number in my own province who are engaged in this profession, I do think it should have been submitted for their consideration so that we may know what they have to say about it.

maintopic: CANADIAN NURSES ASSOCIATION.
speechtext: The Bill has been before the House for nearly two months. If the hon. gentleman (Mr. Johnston, Cape Breton) represents a Nova Scotia constituency I have no doubt he has sent copies of the Bill to his constituents, and if any complaints have reached him he might present them to the House. He had an opportunity of doing so on two occasions when the Bill was in committee. I may say that a lady who occupies a very prominent position amongst the nurses of Nova Scotia appears among the incorporators. That, I suppose, may be taken as some indication that the nursing-profession in Nova Scotia is not at all hostile to the measure. If the hon. gentleman (Mr. Johnston, Cape Breton) will point out wherein the nursing profession, or any member of it, will be injured by the passage of the Biil I shall be very glad to hear him.

maintopic: CANADIAN NURSES ASSOCIATION.
speechtext: This Bill incorporates a purely voluntary association. As originally introduced one of the provisions of the Bill excluded from membership a large number of nurses, who, many hon. members thought, ought to be eligible. The House then referred the Bill back to the Private Bills Committee for further consideration. The Bill was amended there by removing the objectionable clause, and now there is no class of nurses in the community excluded from eligibility for membership in this voluntary association, nor is there any special privileges conceded to the members of this association which differentiates them from other nurses engaged in nursing throughout Canada, except that they are members of the association. The Bill received a thorough threshing out in the committee, a long discussion in the House, and the objectionable clause having been removed I think it ought to pass.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

maintopic: CANADIAN NURSES ASSOCIATION.
speechtext: Might I ask, what are the provisions of the Bill as it now stands with regard to membership in the association.

maintopic: CANADIAN NURSES ASSOCIATION.
speechtext: As clause 5 stands now, all nurses engaged in professional work and graduated and holding certificates from any incorporated hospital in Canada, or from any hospital under the control of any provincial government or any municipality in Canada, or who have graduated and hold certificates from any other hospital approved of by the association, and which gives not less than two years training to nurses before granting certificates; shall be eligible.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

maintopic: CANADIAN NURSES ASSOCIATION.
speechtext: A further section of the Bill ought to be read, and it will give the House a better opportunity of knowing what the qualifications are. There is a second examination required in order to qualify.

maintopic: CANADIAN NURSES ASSOCIATION.
CANADIAN NURSES ASSOCIATION.
speechtext:
Oh, but there is. If my hon. friend will read the Bill, he will find that this association has power to prescribe a second examination from nurses even though they have graduated from certain well-recognized hospitals in this country.
Hon. Mr. ROSS (Victoria, N.S.) This Bill was sent back to the committee a second time, and every objection that was raised in the House, including that raised by the hon. member for North Oxford (Mr. Sutherland), was removed ; and he stated to myself that he was now perfectly satisfied with the Bill. The hon. member for West Toronto removed every objection so that the Bill should be made acceptable to the whole Dominion, and as one member from the province of Nova Scotia I do not think there is anything to be feared from its passing.

maintopic: CANADIAN NURSES ASSOCIATION.
speechtext: When this Bill came before the committee, I was one of those most strongly opposed to it ; but the objectionable clauses were eliminated. The hon. member for Cape Breton (Mr. Johnston) says there are too many examinations. That matter was arranged in this manner. By clause 6 the board may require an examination. The word 1 may ' is put in there purposely. But clause 5 says that the members of the association shall consist of nurses holding certificates of not less than two years standing. This gives every such nurse the right to join the association ; but in case there are any disabilities or conditions justifying an examination, the saving clause is put in providing that an examination may be held. Everything objectionable in the Bill, so far as I can see, has been removed, and I agree entirely with the Minister of Marine and Fisheries that the Bill as it now stands should be passed. I believe the association is practically a voluntary association for the benefit of the nurses.

maintopic: CANADIAN NURSES ASSOCIATION.
speechtext: I want to ask the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, who appears to know all about this Bill, whether it places the hospital of Charlottetown on the same level as it now occupies ?

maintopic: CANADIAN NURSES ASSOCIATION.
speechtext: I do not understand that this Bill places the graduates of any hospital in Canada under any disqualification whatever. Trained nurses graduating from any hospital in Canada are eligible for membership ; but some members wanted to include graduates from hospitals in the United States, and therefore an amendment was proposed that the president of the medical board of each province might require them to pass an examination in addition to the certificate they held.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

maintopic: CANADIAN NURSES ASSOCIATION.
speechtext: I may say further that the nurses in the hospital in Charlottetown are all eligible for membership provided they pass a certain examination.

maintopic: CANADIAN NURSES ASSOCIATION.
speechtext: That is not necessary.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

maintopic: CANADIAN NURSES ASSOCIATION.
speechtext: The association can exact it.

maintopic: CANADIAN NURSES ASSOCIATION.
speechtext: My hon. friend is wrong there. The association cannot exact it, hut the president of the medical society of the province may require an examination.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

maintopic: CANADIAN NURSES ASSOCIATION.
speechtext: I want the Minister of Marine and Fisheries to read the section, and then he will better understand what the requirements are.

maintopic: CANADIAN NURSES ASSOCIATION.
speechtext: I want to ask the hon. member for West Toronto if this Bill will exclude from membership those persons who ihave been doing work as nurses for a quarter of a century, and are not now in a position to obtain certificates.

maintopic: CANADIAN NURSES ASSOCIATION.
speechtext: There are many excellent nurses who are not in a position to undergo examination before the medical board-who know very little about the technical subjects of anatomy and physiology and the materia medica in the abstract, but who, nevertheless, are perfectly capable of doing all the work required of them. These ladies, though they have not studied these subjects in the training schools, have nevertheless, acquired by practical experience all the proficiency desired. It is not really a technical knowledge of these various branches that constitutes a really good nurse. A patient, painstaking, kindly attendant at the bedside is really the successful nurse, and no one in this parliament would debar such ladies, who besides have considerable skill and experience, from practicing their profession.

maintopic: CANADIAN NURSES ASSOCIATION.
speechtext: This Bill does not exclude nurses from practicing their profession in any part of the country, even if they should not belong to this association. This Bill is merely to incorporate an association of nurses which no one is compelled to join.

maintopic: CANADIAN NURSES ASSOCIATION.
speechtext: I move that the chairman leave the Chair.

maintopic: CANADIAN NURSES ASSOCIATION.
speechtext: Before that motion is put, I wish to make a few remarks. When this matter came before the committee some two or three weeks ago, the object of the Bill seemed to be approved of, but the objection was raised that it might result in the establishment of a close corporation which would give its own members a certain prestige, to the detriment of others. The -chief discussion in the committee was over the limitation of the number of beds in the hospital. That limitation has been entirely removed, and now it seems to me that the provisions of the Bill are perfectly proper. The Bill provides that the corporation may insist on an examination. It seems to me perfectly proper that that examination shall be conducted by the provincial medical board.

maintopic: CANADIAN NURSES ASSOCIATION.
speechtext: I think that nurses should have some qualifications beyond patience and sweetness. We would not be willing to have nurses who did not possess these qualifications, but, in addition, it would be fair to require that they should have some special qualifications beyond these.

maintopic: CANADIAN NURSES ASSOCIATION.
speechtext:
What information have we that the parties applying for this Bill are really qualified nurses? They will become members if this Bill passes, and then have the right to say who shall be members and who shall not. Yet, we have nothing to prove that they are qualified themselves. There are many nurses, scattered throughout the North-west, who have been practicing their profession there during the last thirty years, and who are just as well qualified as any who have passed or may pass an examination under this Bill, and yet they would be excluded. This Bill has not been sufficiently considered. When it was before the committee, the Railway Committee was sitting, and a great many members of the Private Bills Committee attended the larger committee, and, consequently, were not present when the various clauses of this Bill were considered. If the measure is to be a success, it should be thoroughly looked into. Let it be referred back to the committee, and taken up next session, and let copies of it be sent in the meantime to the various hospitals and nursing institutions throughout the country, and thus give these institutions an opportunity of expressing their opinion on its various features. We all know what the position is in the medical profession. A man thoroughly qualified and authorized to practice is in one province, and cannot practice in another, and the same remark applies to the legal profession ; and the reason is just because such Bills as this were put through the local and federal parliaments without proper consideration. If this measure is to apply to the whole of Canada, all the people interested should have an opportunity of understanding what it means. Those ladies who have given the best part of their lives to a profession of nursing throughout the west- I refer to the nuns and sisters of mercy-should be allowed to become members of this proposed association purely on that ground alone, if they so desired, and not be compelled to undergo an examination at the dictates of a favoured few who form a close corporation.

An advisory board for the government of the Association shall he selected at each annual meeting. therein, may impose penalties for unprofessional conduct

It is a star chamber, you see.

It remains for these ladies to trump up a case against any lady or body of ladies whom they do not choose to have in their charmed circle. Now, in reply to the hon. member for Annapolis (Mr. Wade), I may say that there is not one trained nurse professionally practicing in Canada but has a certificate of competency from some recognized training school for nurses or some hospital. For my part, as a medical man, I consider these training schools and hospital authorities infinitely better authorities from whom to secure a license to nurse than a mere group of medical men practicing anywhere in the Dominion of Canada. They may know physiology, materia medica, anatomy, they may know all the book learning of the profession, but I would infinitely prefer a certificate of the body managing a respectable hospital than the certificate of any group of medical men in the Dominion in private practice, as I have just indicated.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAXATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY LANDS.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before you leave the Chair, I wish to make a brief reference to a subject of very considerable importance, the question of the exemption from taxation of the Canadian Pacific Railway land grant. Owing to . a very painful mission to Winnipeg when this question came up last time, I was unable to be present and participate in the debate which took place on this very important question. As a result of the debate, a resolution was passed by this House, authorizing the government to obtain from the courts a judical interpretation as to the duration of this period of exemption from taxation of the Canadian Pacific Railway lands. I think it was very unfortunate that this resolution passed this House. The debates that have occurred make it very clear that if this question is submitted to the courts for judicial decision, the 'courts will not go outside of the technical reading of the clause in question, and there is very grave doubt as to what view the court will take. Hon. gentlemen, and some of them members of the cabinet, hold it to be the reading of that clause that the exemption period shall run for twenty years from the time at which these lands were patented. I learned with
satisfaction from the speech made by the Minister of the Interior that the patents are being issued for these lands, and, in a very short time all the patents will be issued. But if the interpretation be that the period of exemption is twenty years from the issue of the patents, the exemption period, instead of being twenty years, as was the intention when the contract was ratified in 1881, will be forty years, and that will be a great hardship and a great injustice to the settlers in the North-west, who confidently believed that when that contract was ratified the exemption period would extend only for twenty years from the ratification of the contract. This is a question where the broad principles laid down so strongly this afternoon by the Minister of Railways and Canals (.Hon. Mr. Blair), the Minister of Finance (Hon. Mr. Fielding) and the right hon. the Prime Minister (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laur-ier) himself should apply.
In the discussion on the additional subsidy for Prince Edward Island we had a proposition laid down that it was a question which must be considered in equity. It was contended that Prince Edward Island had no legal claim, but we had the declaration made that whatever be the claim Prince Edward Island might have it had at least a moral claim, and that it should be settled in equity. Now I take it that if there is any question before the parliament of Canada at the present day which ought to be settled in equity, it is this question of the taxation of the Canadian Pacific Railway lands. I read with considerable interest the proposition made by the leader of the opposition in this House when the debate occurred recently, that the lands should be taxed and faith kept with the settlers of the North-west, and if the Canadian Pacific Railway feels aggrieved, or thinks it is entitled to compensation, then the parliament of Canada should take into consideration the question of such compensation as it might think proper. But I think at least all fair-minded men, all reasonable men, will agree that we ought to deal justly with the people of the North-west, that inasmuch as it appears from the debates which occurred when that contract was before parliament, that members on both sides of the House took the position that the exemption period was for twenty years only, and inasmuch as the people of the North-west settled there under the belief that the exemption period only extended for that time, we ought to keep faith with these settlers and say that the exemption period terminates at the end of twenty years from the ratification of the contract. Hon. gentlemen who listened to the debates which have occurred in this House from time to time will recollect that a very strong case was made out in favour of the expiration of the exemption in twenty years, not from the ratification of the contract. I myself was able to quote from a

speech by Sir Hector Langevin, then Minister of Public Works, in which he declared that within twenty years from the date of that contract no lands would remain exempted from taxation other than the roadway 100 feet wide through which the railway runs. I was able to quote from the speech of the then member for West Middlesex, Mr. Ross, now the hon. premier of Ontario, also frofn Mr. Rinfret, from the present Minister of Customs (Hon. Mr. Paterson) and from many others, quotations which clearly indicated that it was in their minds that the exemption period would expire in twenty years from the ratification of the contract. Now, Sir, I say that we ought to keep faith with the people there, and if we refer this matter to the courts, as parliament in its wisdom determined should be done, it is at least probable that the courts will decide on. a technical reading of the clause, and may decide upon the interpretation held by many members of the House and by some members of the government, that the twenty-year period dates from the issuing of the patents. Now if they did that it would be decided on a technicality, and that is the danger of submitting this matter to the courts. Parliament should interpret this matter itself, or failing to pass an Act of Interpretation

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAXATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY LANDS.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman has no right to criticise a decision rendered by the House unless he intends to make a motion to reconsider. He must abstain from making any remarks upon the judgment of the House.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAXATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY LANDS.
speechtext: I am glad you corrected me, Mr. Speaker. I am not well versed in these mattters, but I will endeavour as far as possible to confine myself within the limits of proper debate. I was going to show that there is danger, if the question were submitted to the courts, that they might give a technical decision, whereas parliament should take all questions into consideration

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAXATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY LANDS.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman has no right to criticise a decision of the House. The decision may be right or wrong, but he has no right to question it.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAXATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY LANDS.
speechtext: Of course I am not asking for a reconsideration. However, I can probably avoid trespassing upon the rule by saying that while I might move for an Act interpreting the clause, I can very well see that I should bow to the decision of parliament when it rejected that.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAXATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY LANDS.
speechtext:
There are occasions when the strict rules of the House are not enforced unless attention is called to them. I would suggest that in view of the desire of the hon. gentleman to bring his views before the House again, the rule be not strictly enforced in this case.
Mr. RICHARDSON (Lisgar) Let me express my thanks to the hon. the Minister Mr. RICHARDSON (Lisgar).
of the Interior for his kind suggestion. I do not wish to trespass upon the rules of the House. But this is a matter in which I take the very deepest interest, and I would like that the very best results should be obtained, and I feel sure that the House desires that we should reach the very best decision in this matter. I was going to say that I hold strongly the opinion that whatever might be. the judicial interpretation of this clause, it would be a great injustice to the people of the North-west if that decision should be that the exemption period should be for forty years instead of twenty, as was the original design when the contract was adopted. I put a question on the Order paper some days ago as to what contention the government would make when the case was submitted to the courts, and the answer I got, while it was not entirely satisfactory, still it might be viewed with satisfaction by many people of the North-west. The minister replied that they would endeavour to make a contention which would be in the best interests of the people of the North-west. Still it seems to me so clear what was intended at the time, that after consulting with my friends and thinking it over for some weeks, I decided to ask the House to pass a resolution requesting the government to make the contention before the courts that the exemption period begins with the ratification of the contract and expires twenty years later. Of course it would meet my views better if the question were not submitted to the courts at all. I contend with all the earnestness that I possess that we ought to deal with this question on the broad basis of equity, and if we have got to pay the Canadian Pacific Railway a yearly amount, or a large amount, to get rid of what may be a technical advantage in the clause, I say that in justice to the people of the North-west we ought to make some arrangement with the Canadian Pacific Railway, if we do not interpret the clause, and we ought to have these lands released to enable the settlers to reap the benefit of a general taxation.
Now parliament is the only body that can do justice in this matter. I understand that the courts would take no cognizance of what the intention might have been, nor, so far as I can learn, will they take any congnizance of the debates which occurred upon the question when the contract was before the House in 1881. That being the case, I emphasize the point that parliament alone can do justice in equity, and is the only body which can deal with this matter. In the use of the word ' grant' I am disposed to believe that a wrong interpretation will be placed upon it. The clause read that the lands should be exempt from taxation for twenty years ' from the grant thereof from the Crown.' Some will contend that the ' grant thereof from the Crown' meant the issue of the patents. Now I

claim that the ' grant thereof from the Grown' meant the gift of the land to the company, and, as 1 contended at some length in a former speech on this question, when the land was granted by statute it belonged to the company as much as if they had received their patents for it. The company applied for the money grants as they became due, but they did not apply for the land, but that was no fault of the settlers, and it might be fairly said it was no fault of this parliament. But what I say is that it was the company's own fault that they did not apply for it before they had 'sold their lands, as if the patents had been issued the day the contract was ratified. That being the case, they received what is known in Great Britain as a grant by a statute, or a gift of land, and it would be unfair to contend that the grant meant the issue of the patents. But the danger is that the courts may construe it to mean that. Such being the case, I contend that we should have this matter settled by parliament and not by the courts.
There is one clause in the contract which reiads that if the lands are either sold or occupied they shall become taxable. These lands become immediately taxable notwithstanding the fact that patents have not been issued for them and therefore, I say, if it applies in one case where there is no patent it is surely fair to assume that it applies in another case. We have been met with the opposition that to pass an interpretation Act would be to interfere with the vested rights of the company. To those who make that contention I would say that in 1894 an Act was introduced into this House by the ex-Minister of Railways and Canals (Hon. Mr. Haggart) for the purpose of interpreting a clause in the Canadian Pacific Railway charter. Under that charter the company was allowed to import all materials required for the original construction of the railway, bridges, &c., free of duty. The company completed the road and in 1896 an order in council was passed declaring the road to be completed, but later on, the company desired to build new bridges and it applied for a drawback of duty on the material required for these bridges. Sir John Thompson, who was then Minister of Justice, reported that inasmuch as the order in council had been passed declaring the road completed it would be impossible to comply with the request and allow the company the drawback, whereupon a Bill was introduced by the hon. ex-Minister of Railways and Canals to this effect :
That it is expedient to provide that the words ' original construction,' in section 1 ot chapter 76 ot the statutes of 1882, respecting the allowance of drawback on certain articles manufactured in Canada, for use in the construction of the Canadian Pacific Railway, shall be construed to extend to and include the first iron or steel bridge erected in a locality, but not to any renewal or repair thereof.
That was a very clear case of the contract
being construed in the interest of the railway company. I read from ' Hansard ' :

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAXATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY LANDS.
speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman please explain ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAXATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY LANDS.
speechtext:
The object of the resolution is to give interpretation to section 1 of chapter 7 of 45 Victoria, which reads :-
Mr. Laurier objected to the proposal, whereupon the late Mr. Dalton McCarthy made some remarks also objecting and declaring that this was an interpretation of the contract and should not pass. Sir John Thompson spoke as follows :
I think that is not exactly the position. Though it is quite proper that any application made, and the correspondence upon it should be brought down, I am afraid that that correspondence is of so meagre a character that it will not throw much light upon the question. But the Canadian Pacific Railway Company's contention is that the expression ' original construction ' includes every original construction on the road that is made of iron or steel. But, the interpretation which I thought we were bound to put on the Act, in order to guard the treasury as much as possible, was that it did not include these structures in consequence of our having declared, for the purpose of the subsidy, that the railway had been finished.
So, as I have said, Sir John Thompson made the declaration that it was necessary to have an Act of interpretation passed in order that the drawback could be allowed. A debate occurred subsequently and the late Mr. Dalton McCarthy used these words:
For my part, I am not willing, and I do not think this House is willing, to change the contract with the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. This is, no matter how it may be disguised, or how it may be introduced to us, simply an alteration of the contract in favour of the company. The contract says in certain terms that the company are entitled to this drawback, or it does not. X understand the opinion of the Department of Justice is that, under the terms of the contract, the company are not entitled to the benefit of this drawback, and certainly that is the view I would have formed as regards the contract by reading the statute. The company are asking, in effect, that they should receive from the government of Canada a drawback of 30 odd per cent upon the value of the bridges which they shall build in substitution of bridges built when the road was first constructed. If we may take the amounts stated in the report, and that is the only information we have, the total outlay will be something like three-quarters of a million dollars, and the amount of the rebate will reach $200,000.

speechtext: It is more than that, because it is necessary to complete the work, and the company has been putting in bridges since 1891.

speechtext:
I am not prepared to alter the contract in one line or one letter. Under the contract the company have been able to float their securities, construct the road and pay dividends, and, according to the contract, as I have said, they are entitled or they are not entitled to get the drawback proposed. I would not deprive the company of a single right under the contract, hut I am not prepared, and, in fact, I do not understand why we should in-

terpret the contract in a different sense from the meaning which its language bears.
Mr. McCarthy spoke as follows, later on :
I think the House will perfectly understand that this alteration in the contract will mean before we are done with it, probably up in the millions.
This is an important statement.
I think we had better realize and understand what we are doing. Of course, that ought to make no difference if the railway company were entitled to the change-because change it is-in the contract which is sought to be made now at the instance of the hon. Minister of Railways. But, for my part, I do not look upon it by any means as a technicality. I look upon it as a substantial change in their contract.
Then, a long debate followed in which many members participated. The hon. member for South Simcoe (Hon. Mr. Tisdale), as I pointed out the other day, urged the House to take a broad view of the question and not rest its decision upon any technicality. Although, when I made my motion in the House previously he took strong ground against it and hoped he would not be a party to interpreting any contract, because he did not think it would be proper in any British country. He, however, in the debate in 1894, from which I have quoted, took strong ground in favour of interpretation. I find that just before the division there is a brief statement by Mr. Mills, of Bothwell, the present hon. Minister of Justice, who said :
I am prepared to oppose what we have a right to oppose, and what is no part of the compact as X understand it, but I am not prepared to alter what I regard as the original intention of both the parliament on the one side and the company on the other.	[DOT]

speechtext: Where do you find that intention ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the Senate

speechtext:
I find it in the statutes and in the discussion that took place at the time the compact between the company and the government was entered into.
So that, according to Mr. Mills, he was governed by the discussion which occurred when the contract was ratified in 1881.
If therefore that was the view of the Minister of Justice at that time, surely the contention which I make is a fair one, namely:	That this parliament should settle the question and should see that the rights of the settlers in that country are protected, and that the exemption does not extend for a longer period than twenty years from the ratification. I have looked over the division list and I find such names as the following who voted in favour of that interpretation :	Mr. Beausoleil, Mr. Bennett, Sir John Carling, Mr. Carroll, Mr. Choquet, Mr. Montague, Mr. Guay, Mr. Haggart, Mr. Harwood, Mr. Laurier, Mr. Livingston, Mr. Maclean (York), Mr. McGregor, Mr. Mignault, Mr. Mills, Mr. Rinfret, Mr. Tarte, Sir John Thompson, Mr. Wilson, and many other prominent men of that day. I find that that Act of interpretation passed by a vote of 100 to 15. If Mr, RICHARDSON (Lisgar).
you could get a vast majority of members of parliament to vote an interpretation in favour of the Canadian Pacific Railway, surely I do not ask an unreasonable thing when I say that the interests of the settlers should be protected, and if to that end we do not get a majority of 80 or 90, surely we could get a majority of this House to do justice to the settlers in this matter. I want to apologize to the House for taking up time at this late period of the session. I have discussed the question once or twice before, and as I have said already it is only the great importance of the question that prompts me at the present time. I beg to move seconded by tbe hon. member for Alberta (Mr. Oliver) :
That this House having, by resolution adopted on the 2nd day ot April last, declared its intention ol obtaining a judicial interpretation of tbe clause in the Canadian Pacific Railway contract relating to the exemption from taxation of the company's land grant, the House now request the government to make the contention before the courts that the exemption period contemplated in the contract began when the contract granting tbe subsidies, both in cash and lands, was ratified by parliament.	. ,
I may say that while it is desirable that the government should make that contention before the courts, I urged it because 1 thought it was the clear intention of parliament when that contract was ratified, and if the government make that contention they will not be debarred from obtaining a more moderate construction of the clause. I think we should at least contend for the most, but as I said at the outset, I greatly regretted, and do still regret that the intention seems to he to refer this matter to the courts. I think it should not be referred to the courts at ail. 1 think it should he dealt with by parliament and justice done to the settlers of that country on the broad basis of the equity of the claim.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAXATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY LANDS.
speechtext:
I do not think that my hon. friend (Mr. Richardson) need apologize for taking up the time of parliament upon this question, because the importance of it is quite sufficient to justify the attention of parliament for the length it has occupied our consideration this session. I cannot see, however, that my hon. friend has added anything to the discussion which took place in the House upon one or two former occasions. I need only reiterate: That the precedents which were referred to, and the precedent which is referred to as having been set this afternoon in the case of Prince Edward Island, were all cases in which the two parties got together and made an agreement as to what should be done. For instance, in connection with the drawback clause in the Canadian Pacific Railway contract, the company and the then government discussed the matter and made an arrangement themselves as to what they

mutually thought the contract meant. Then the government, for fear that might not be held to be the legal construction of the contract and in order to protect themselves in the carrying out of their view, brought legislation to parliament for the purpose of making that clear. There was no precedent there for the alteration or determination or interpretation of a contract by parliament against the wishes of one of the parties to the contract. That is so clear that it would be sheer waste of time to discuss it longer. My hon. friend refers to the possibility of this House considering the question of compensation for the loss sustained by the settlers of the North-west in not being able to tax these lands at the time when it was anticipated they would be able to tax them, but that is a question which is not before us and which I submit cannot come before us until we actually know what this contract means, and what the courts shall decide it does mean. So far as the resolution is concerned, I think it would be manifestly unwise for the House to attempt to bind the government in that connection. I am quite free to say now, as I said the other day, that if the law officers of the Crown; counsel employed by the Crown or the Minister of Justice, should advise the government that there is any reasonable prospect of success in making the contention that the period from which the twenty years began to run dates from the period when the contract was ratified by parliament; the government will be only too happy to make that contention before the court. But in the absence of a full and deliberate consideration of the matter by the law officers of the Crown, I think every person in the House will agree that it would be unwise for the House, upon a motion the exact terms of which the government have not been able to consider, and of which the government had no notice until it was read by the hon. gentleman

speechtext: Exactly. The motion has been published in the Votes and Proceedings for two or three weeks.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAXATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY LANDS.
speechtext:
I must admit that the notice has escaped my attention. The matter has been under discussion several times, and I assume that the notice escaped my attention owing to the fact that there were many proceedings taken on the same matter, and I was not aware that a new resolution was to be moved. I still say that I think it would be manifestly unwise for the House to bind the government in a legal proceeding to a course which might, in the opinion of the law advisers of the government, be considered unwise, and not likely to result in a successful issue. The question has been in one form or another before the courts on more than one occasion. There was a case tried in the province of Manitoba in which there was a dissenting judgment given by the present Chief Justice of that province, who is a very able jurist. He discussed the whole question at very great length and with very great ability. There is nothing in that judgment, I am bound to say, that wmuld justify the contention that the period from which the twenty years would run began with the ratification of the contract. There is much in the reasoning of the Chief Justice which would lead to the conclusion that the point might be safely taken, that the period of twenty years began to run from the time when the lands were actually earned, and when the government therefore would have been in a position to satisfy the demand in the clause of the contract which provides for the exemption, and grant the lands from the Crown. In view of the whole position I feel it is the duty of the government to take the ground that this resolution ought not to pass, and that the government ought not to be bound as to the terms of the reference. I say again that the government will endeavour to place the matter before the courts in such a way as to get the most favourable interpretation possible.
Mi;. FRANK OLIVER (Alberta). I am very sorry to delay the House at this date of the session, but the question is of such very overwhelming importance in the district I represent that I would not be justified in allowing this opportunity to pass without expressing my views upon the subject. When the question was brought before the House on a former occasion, the House decided not to interpret the statute. What I desired on that occasion was, and what I desire on this occasion is, to put before the House the reasons why the lands should be held to be taxable twenty years after the Act was passed, that is to say, to give reasons why the land should be held to be taxable after the 15th of February last. I feel that it would not be fair to let the idea go before the country that because the House was not willing to agree to the interpretation of a contract, the position which I took then, and which I take now, was, therefore, unsound. 1 maintained then, as I maintain now, that there is only one interpretation to that statute-that there is not now and never was any reason to doubt what that interpretation is. I have been no party to raising any doubt as to the meaning of the statute. I was surprised beyond measure when I heard that there was any doubt upon it, and I have been still more surprised since to find that members of the House, to whose legal knowledge and ability I am bound to pay great respect, do consider that there is a doubt as to the meaning of the statute. It is not because of any doubt I

hold, but it is because of the doubts they hold, that I desire now to put the case before the House as I understand it.
There are three contentions in regard to the date of expiry of this exemption ; one, that it expires twenty years from the passing of the Act; another, that it expires twenty years after the lands were earned under the Act; and, third, that it expires twenty years after the issue of the patent. There is a great deal of difference to the people of the North-west in the result of these several contentions. Under the first contention, the twenty years exemption has already expired, and the lands have now become taxable as soon as the patents are issued ; under the second contention the lands will not become taxable for some years yet, which I contend is contrary to the letter and spirit of the Act, and is to that extent unjust to the people of the North-west; while the third contention, in my humble judgment, is utterly absurd-is not tenable on any grounds whatever. I hope I say that with all due respect to those who hold a different view. Such a contention is so utterly contrary to anything that was in contemplation in the mind of parliament or in the mind of the country at the time the Act was passed, that I cannot see how it can be held. To hold that twenty years means forty years is, it seems to me, the height of absurdity. The fair question, as it appears to me, is whether the exemption expired on the 15th of February last or whether it shall expire twenty years from the date when the lands were severally earned. I take the liberty of arguing now that the exemption did, as a matter of fact, according to the letter and the spirit of the Act, expire on the 15th of February last. The whole question turns on the meaning of a single word-the word ' grant.' The question is whether that word means ' gift ' or means ' patent.' I hold that the word ' grant ' is entitled to be used in the ordinary dictionary meaning of 1 gift,' and is not entitled to be used in the technical or legal meaning of ' patent.'
In support of that contention, I read an extract from a report of the committee of the hon. the Privy Council, dated the 20th of February, 1900, relating to the land grant of the North-west Central Railway, in which the word ' grant ' occurs. From this I hope to establish my point as to the usual and ordinary meaning of the word ' grant ' : and the meaning which is attached to it in orders in council and other government documents similar to Acts of parliament. This report states that on the 22nd of July, 1880, an order in council was passed authorizing the grant of a charter ; that on the same date an order in council was passed granting the charter; and that on the same date an order in council was passed authorizing the grant to the company of a land subsidy of 0,400 acres a mile. In the first two instances the word ' grant is Mr. OLIVER.
used as ' gift,' and there is no reason to say that in the third case the word ' grant ' is not used as ' gift.' It certainly cannot be used as ' patent.' However, in this case the words used authorize a grant, and it may be held that in that case the grant is not actually made. But, as a matter of fact, the grant is actually made by this very order in council authorizing the grant. The same paragraph goes on to say :
The grant to consist of the unoccupied and unclaimed odd-numbered sections within ten miles of the line of railway on either side thereof in so far as practicable without interfering with any previous grants or reserves.
That means that that land was granted then by that order in council, because it was reserved and preserved from any other occupation or ownership by that order in council then issued. I say that in that case the word ' grant ' meant the gift of that land, and it did not mean, and could not be construed to mean, patent. Then, further down, in a subsequent paragraph, the order in council recites that ' the company having forfeited any further rights it might have acquired in respect thereto.' What rights it had it forfeited at that time ; therefore, the land was not patented to it. To make that binding, a subsequent paragraph says that ' no land has so far been passed to the company.' So, the word ' grant ' has been used in all the preceding part of the document, and here in this paragraph, which says that ' so far no land has been passed to the company,' the word 1 passed ' is used as synonymous with the word ' patent.' Further on, this document recites: 'The annexed schedule of land be substituted in lieu thereof, in satisfaction of the land grant to the North-west Central Railway.' If I read the English language correctly, the land was granted, and this land was scheduled in satisfaction of that grant. The grant was made when the order in council was passed, and was satisfied when the lands were scheduled to the company. But, that was not when the grant was made. It was made in the beginning, when the land was reserved to the company, that is to say, when the order in council wTas passed.
In conclusion I read from the heading : ' Schedule of lands granted to the company,' the words ' lands granted to the Great Northwest Central Railway west of the first meridian.' There again the word * grant ' is used and yet the patents had not been issued for any of those lands, so far as this order in council is concerned. I make the contention then, that the use of the word ' grant ' in Acts of parliament or orders in council is not interchangeable with the word ' patent,' I make the contention that there is not any doubt whatever as to the meaning of that Act of parliament, and the proof I claim is contained in this as it would be in any other order in council that might be issued or Act that might be passed.

Here is a list of the lands which have been granted, and not an acre of those has been patented, although they are said to have been granted, were at first granted by order in council, and now are scheduled or listed in pursuance of the grant then made. All we ask is that the government shall make a contention that is according to the letter and spirit of the law, and in the public interest, not only of the western territory, but of Canada as a whole.
It is not only the western settler who is at a loss because of the exemption from taxation. Mention has been made of compensation to be demanded on the one hand or paid on the other because of this exemption. Possibly the House is not aware that such compensation has been paid every year. Consideration has been given in estimating the amount of grant to the North-west Territories ; and because the schools and the roads of the Territories are not able to secure that general taxation upon the whole land owned in the country which is their due, the subsidy has been increased accordingly. And let me tell the House that the subsidy will have to be still further and very largely increased, if the needs of the country are to be met, on account of this very exemption.

I would like to say a few words in connection with this matter. With reference to the arguments set up by the last speaker, I quite agree with him in many respects, but I submit his arguments should be used before the courts and not this House. What are the facts ? There is a contract between the government and the railway corporation, and the question comes up as to the interpretation of a certain portion of the contract. The government may think that the views of my bon. friend are right and that these lands should be subject to taxation from the loth of February last, or may hold that the lands were granted when earned. But the other parties to the contract dispute these contentions and say that these lands are not subject to taxation until twenty years from the date that the patents are issued. What, then, is the government to do ? My hon. friend who moved this resolution, and my hon. friend who has just spoken, discussed the matter on several occasions in this House and a vote was taken, and they know that the House by a great majority decided against their resolution. I then moved a resolution on the 2nd April to have the question as to when these lands became taxable submitted to the courts. I have no doubt that the whole thing hinges on the interpretation of the word ' grant,' and that the general consensus of opinion in this House is that the lands were granted when earned some twenty years ago, and I have no doubt that the court shall so decide. In discussing this question the hon. Minister of the Interior stated that the government were prepared, whenever any school district or
municipality assessed a certain portion of the Canadian Pacific Railway land and their assessment was disputed, to pay the expenses of carrying the matter into the courts, even so far as the Privy Council, in which case we would have a decision to go on. That is the only way it can be settled. The hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Richardson) said he did not want this case submitted to the courts because he was afraid of them. Well, he is the first man I ever heard say that he was afraid of the courts in this country. Does he put his judgment against that of the courts ? If so, I am afraid that he will not find many who will agree with him. Why is he afraid of the courts ? Because the debates on the question in this House might influence the Supreme Court and the Privy Council of Great Britain. I do not take that view. I do not think that the courts are going to be guided by any debates in this House. I believe that if this case comes before them, they will decide it on its merits, and I am satisfied that their decision will be in favour of the people and against the railway corporation.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAXATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY LANDS.
speechtext: It is going to be decided without regard to what the understanding of parliament was. That is what I complain about. We are told by the Solicitor General and the Minister of Finance that the courts will decide on the reading of the clause itself without regard to what parliament intended.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAXATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY LANDS.
speechtext:
When the case comes before the courts, we shall haive our counsel there, and they will take up all phases of the question and place them before the court, and all these matters will be taken into consideration in coming to a final decision. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Richardson) said that he was sorry that this resolution has passed the House. I believe that this resolution, which was proposed by myself, is a step in the right direction. speechtext: Before you leave the Chair, I wish briefly to call the attention of the Minister of Railways and Canals to the strike that has occurred in the locomotive works at Kingston. I understand that at. these works a number of locomotives are being constructed for the Department of Railways and Canals for use on the Intercolonial Railway. I understand also that there will be a bonus given to the company for having some of these locomotives completed by a certain time. It appears that this necessity has led to the company offering piece work and premiums to its employees, and that this system has operated very injuriously. I am informed, and my correspondent is the secretary of the Ironworkers' Union in that city, that the operation of this system has resulted very detrimentally to the principle, as he puts it, of a fair day's work for a fair day's pay. It appears that with the object of getting 'extra work out of the men so that these engines may be turned out on time, the men are induced to perform extra labour for less remuneration even than they should be receiving for a full day's work. This has resulted in a strike of ISO iron workers, and their stoppage of work has necessarily caused the stoppage of work of over 200 other men, so there are now 400 men on strike in that city. The question I wish to put to the Minister of Railways and Canals is this : Does the contract for these engines contain the current-wage clause ? I fear not. If it did, I think there would have been little possibility of this trouble arising. You will remember, Sir, that at the last session of this parliament this House practically instructed the members of the government, in letting contracts, to include this current-wage clause. It seems to me here is a case where it should have been put in, and if it had been put in it is probable there would have been no trouble at the present time. I would also suggest to the acting Minister of Labour, seeing that this factory is now employed on government work, that it would be well, perhaps, to send the deputy minister or an agent down there to see if something could not be done in the way of conciliation before the trouble goes any further. It is a serious matter for the city of Kingston to have 400 men on strike, and I should imagine too it is a serious matter for the Department of Railways and Canals, who want to get their engines as soon as possible.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAXATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY LANDS.
speechtext:
I cannot say that I quite apprehend my hon. friend's purpose in making a reference to me, or what results he thinks could be achieved. I understand that he is of opinion that it would have been well to incorporate in the
contract made by the government with the Kingston Locomotive Works Company what is called the ordinary labour clause, and that if it had been done it might have enabled the Department of Labour to intervene effectively in the present difficulty. If that is my hon. friend's view, I cannot say that I entirely agree with him that the inclusion of that clause would have enabled anybody to avoid the trouble which he says has arisen among the workmen in that city. I gathered from what he stated, as near as I could hear him, that the trouble has arisen out of the action of the company in offering special inducements to certain of their workmen to work longer hours with a view of hastening the completion of the locomotives which they are now building for the government. If that has been che cause of the trouble, I cannot see that any clause which could have been incorporated in the contract insisting that the labour should be paid fair wages, would have bettered the case for the men. The complaint is not that any of the men employed are paid below the current rate of wages for such work, but that some are, in effect, being paid more than the current rate of wages. That appears to be the case, if I gathered correctly the purport of the hon. gentleman's statement. I do not think that the inclusion of that clause in the contract would have benefited the position of the men, or would have enabled anybody to intervene with any hope of success. I am not at all sure that the contract which we made with that company is one that could be drawn so as to include that clause he refers to. There are a good many conditions to be considered in connection with 'work of that kind that would add to the difficulties of working out such a clause. I am well assured of that, because the company have been offering inducements to the men to work harder and to work longer hours under their contract, but that is not a fact which could be pointed to as a violation of any such clause. I think every one will agree that it is most unfortunate that this difficulty has arisen. I am also certain that anything the acting minister can do, if the proper conditions exist to justify his intervention, he will be only too glad to do. There is nothing that I can see that the Department of Railways can do in the matter, and I am unable to offer my hon. friend any encouragement from my department, though I think that if there is anything the acting Minister of Labour can do, he would be very glad to tender his friendly offices.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, before you leave the Chair, I desire to bring to the attention of the government and of the House a few facts relating to the Trent Valley canal. It is not my intention to discuss the wisdom or utility of that great undertaking, the value of which has already been recognized by the governments of both political parties. The former government initiated the work and the present government from time to time are, with the sanction of parliament, appropriating sums of the money looking towards the completion of it. I intend to confine the few remarks I have to make to a statement in reference to the southern end of the canal; that is, to the proposed outlet from Rice Lake to Lake Ontario. It is well known that the proposed outlet to Lake Ontario has always been by the Trent river, and I desire to place a few facts before the House and the government to show that in my opinion, at least, Port Hope is the proper place for that outlet. Quite a number of non. gentlemen who represent constituencies in this House are thoroughly conversant with the ground through which this canal runs, but those hon. gentlemen who are not familiar with the geographical features of this portion of the proposed canal, I will give a short explanation of those features. Rice lake, which lies almost midway between Port Hope and Peterborough, is a lake of about 18 miles in length running

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAXATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY LANDS.
speechtext: Does not Mr. Rogers explain ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAXATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY LANDS.
speechtext:
I can find no explanation in the report. There is simply the statement in his estimate, that the amount of earth excavation is 5.500,000 cubic yeards and the amount of rock excavation 175,000 yards, which bears about the same proportion to the amount of rock excavation in Mr. Main-gy's report, as does the amount of earth excavation. Mr. Rogers further estimates the Frankford section of the canal, that is the nearest section to Trenton, at $750,000,

while Mr. Rubidge, another government engineer, estimates that section to cost $1,200,000, or a trifling difference of half a million. Perhaps the hon. Minister of Railways can explain the difference between these two estimates. Mr. Rogers offers no explanation, but simply states that his estimate is $750,000, -while Mr. Rubidge places it at $1,200,000. Again, Mr. Rogers in his estimate puts in almost everything that can possibly be required for completing the canal by way of Port Hope, such as the buying of the harbour, the repairing of the wharfs, &c., which he places at $300,000. But there is not a word said about the harbour of Trenton. 1 believe that the harbour of Trenton has not anything like the depth that the harbour of Port Hope has, and there are no docks there. In all fairness Mr. Rogers should have put iu his report as to the cost of the Trent Valley section, certain expenditure to correspond with that he has estimated in regard to Port Hope. Perhaps I should have stated that in his report he says that the caDal by way of Port Hope will cost just one million dollars more than by way of the Trent river route. My object in comparing the. two reports is to show that Mr. Rogers has not made the same comparative estimate for the Trent river as he has for the Port Hope route. In order to get $2,800,000 as the cost of the Trent river section he takes his own estimate of $750,000 for the Prank-ford section, and he adapts exactly Mr. Rubidge's estimate of the Hoard's creek section which is $2,078,000. He makes no estimate whatever as to the cost of making the remainder of the Trent river navigable. I understand there is a large portion of that river which will require blasting in order to make it navigable. He makes no estimate whatever as to the cost of lands that will be drowned or for lands for right of way.
In all these features of his report, I say he has not been fair to Port Hope in that he has put all these items of expenditure necessary by the Port Hope route, and has taken no notice whatever of them in his estimate for the route by the Trent river.

Ward) will permit me to ask him if he will be good enough_to refer to Mr. Roger's serious objection to the Port Hope route, upon the ground that there is a long mileage there in which small craft .such as will use the canal, would be exposed to the stoi'ms of Lake Ontario; whereas if the ordinary route via the Trent is used there would be protection afforded by the islands all the way down to Lachine.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAXATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY LANDS.
speechtext: I propose to deal with that question, and I might as well take it up now. The hon. minister will remember that five or six weeks ago an influential deputa-

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAXATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY LANDS.
speechtext:
tion waited upon him from, Campbellford, Trenton, Peterborough, Lindsay and other places. By the courtesy of some of its members I was allowed to attend with that deputation, although I- had no opportunity of making any statement there. The minister will recall to mind that in all the speeches before him-possibly with the exception of that of Mr. Dumble, who spoke about the Trent river canal being possibly a rival to the Erie canal-not one of those gentle-imen who addressed the hon. minister on that occasion spoke in any other way of it, but as a route for local traffic. I think this is an answer to the objection that is made in regard to the haul between Port Hope and the Murray canal. I remember how very strongly these gentlemen urged that Peterborough was becoming quite a manufacturing centre and that the large manufacturing interests there required this canal to be built as they should have an outlet to Lake Ontario. In that connection I would bring the attention of the minister to the fact, that at Port Hope there are already three elevators which are quite capable of handling the grain traffic which would come in that direction. I can also point out to the minister, that for this local traffic the freight-would naturally seek an outlet to the city of Toronto, and by the Port Hope route, Peterborough and the districts surrounding is 87 miles nearer Toronto than by way of the Trent river.
There is another consideration which I would bring to the attention of the Minister of Railways and Canals, and that is, that Oak Orchard on the American side is only 39 miles distant from Port Hope, and that there have been frequent discussions about eistablishing a system of very large ferryboats running direct from Oak Orchard to Port Hope, with the idea of the coal supply being brought there for distribution in the country to the north. That is another evidence that Port Hope -would be the proper place for that particular end of the canal, for this reason, that the barges which would bring coal across that short distance of thirty-nine miles, and which would not go by the canal, would be able to tranship the coal at Port Hope, so that it could be landed at Peterborough by a route eighty-three miles shorter than by the Trent river route.
And another thing, Mr. Speaker, by the Trent river route it is necessary to cross railways five times, whereas, going by way of Port Hope, the canal can go under the viaduct, and there is not one crossing really needed ; the advantage of this in the working of the canal is apparent.
I have simply brought these few facts to the attention of the government, with the idea that if they are looked carefully into, and the different reports upon the subject are carefully compared, the government will be inclined before deciding on one route or the other to have a report made by an entirely independent engineer. I do not mean

to attribute to Mr. Rogers the favouring of one route over the other ; but I simply say that from his long association with the canal projected in the other direction, he might possibly have a little bias. I do not go beyond that but I think that the fact of all these discrepancies between his report and the other reports would justify the government in having a report from an independent engineer before a definite conclusion is arrived at, and I would strongly urge the government to do that in justice and fairness to the town of Port Hope. The hon. minister will remember that quite an influential deputation waited upon him, I think, last year, and urged the claims of Port Hope in connection with the canal, and probably most of these facts were then brought to his attention, and I think the hon. minister held out some hopes to the deputation that if it should be found that Port Hope was the natural outlet for the canal, and that its construction could be accomplished a great deal more cheaply in that direction, possibly something would be done-at any rate, that it would be given full consideration before a decision was come to. That is all I ask of the government-that full consideration should be given to the claims of Port Hope, and that the report of an independent engineer should be had before a final conclusion is arrived at.

speechtext:
I am very glad to hear the hon. member for East Durham (Mr. Ward) discuss the Trent Valley canal ; but I suppose he understands that the idea of the canal going by Port Hope is regarded in this House as a joke, because the distance by that route would be very much longer than by the Trent river, which is the natural route for the canal. Moreover, if the canal went by Port Hope, the damage to the flow of the river would be very great all the way down to the mouth. I have always heard that the engineers favoured the route by the Trent river, and I am very much surprised to hear the hon. member for East Durham advocating the Port Hope route, though I know he is speaking in the interest of his constituents. The hon. gentleman claims that the distance to Toronto via Port Hope would be eighty-seven miles shorter than via Trenton ; but the distance to Montreal would be that much greater. The route by Port Hope would really be a roundabout route. I do not think the hon. gentleman expects that the canal will ever go by Port Hope ; he might as well talk of it going by Toronto. Then, the dangerous part of the lake is between Port Hope and Trenton. I will not object to any surveys being made of the route to Port Hope, because X know that when the Minister of Railways and Canals looks over it, he will see that that is not the proper way, even if it is shorter to the city of Toronto. The object of the canal is not to run to the city of Toronto, but to form part of 171	[DOT]
a through route from the Georgian Bay to the city of Montreal. When the Trent Valley canal is built, I believe it will be equal to the Erie canal. I do not wish to discuss the matter further than simply to protest against the suggestion of the hon. member for East Durham in favour of the canal going by Port Hope.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAXATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY LANDS.
speechtext: I would like to ask the hon. gentleman if the diversion of the water would not be the same by running the canal across the neck of land at what is known as Hoard's creek ? Would not the diversion of the water cause damage there as well ?

I hope the House will allow me to make a reference to the strike at Kingston. Not that I desire to force myself on the House, but I think I ought to state the facts of the case. The strike was sudden and entirely unexpected by the proprietors of the Kingston Locomotive Works. The labourers made a

demand against the company for 10 cents per day increase in their wages. I may add that the strike is entirely confined to the labourers and does not extend to the other classes of workmen. The labourers were already paid from $1.20 to $1.65 per day. The superintendent was out of town, and the proprietors asked that the limit of ten days-which was given in the ultimatum of the labourers, after which they declared they would go on strike if their demand was not acceded to-be extended. They had every reason to believe that this request for an extension would be granted because of the very pleasant relations which hitherto had existed between them and the men. However, no answer was given, and on the 16th the men went on strike, which involved practically the closing of all the works, as the machinists could not work when the labourers did not.
While my sympathies would naturally be; with the men, if they are underpaid, I think it but fair that I should put before the House the case of the proprietors, as it was stated in last night's papers by Mr. Birmingham, one of the managers :
We received no reply to the answer we sent the union or any intimation that our answer was unsatisfactory until we found that the men were on strike. We have no fight with the machinists. The premium system is now in operation in all the shops. The men have asked for it. Through its workings the amount of wages paid the men has increased 17 per cent since January. In some cases we have already decided upon an increase. In other cases, we have decided not to grant an increase. We propose to pay as much as similar labourers get in other shops. It seems extraordinary that we should be singled out by the unions, when the Kingston foundry pays only $1.10 a day for the same work as we pay $1.20 for. The fact is, we are paying higher wages to labourers than similar labourers in other institutions are receiving. We told the committee this morning that the men could stay out or come back, just as they liked. A committee representing the striking union waited upon the company this morning and were given an audience. President Flanigan explained that the company's reply to their demands had been favourably considered, but the company's 'action in discharging one Connolly yesterday had precipitated the trouble. The union thought other men would be discharged to-day, more next day and so on, until the power of the union would be broken.
That is practically the position of tbe matter to-day. While I admit that the Minister of Labour, under tbe recent Act, lias no authority to act in a matter of this kind, it seems to me that bis mediation might very well be offered. Although tbe labouring men believe that their wages are too small, these wages are larger than are paid for similar work in other shops, and the employers declare that they have decided upon a certain advance, so that very likely, even without any intervention, the trouble will come to a speedy termination. But I agree with tbe bon. member for Winnipeg that the best way to settle these difficulties is to Mr. BHITTON.
act promptly, and I hope that the acting Minister of Labour will offer his services as mediator at this juncture and that tbe difficulty will be brought to a close.

It might be desirable to know to what extent Mr. O'Donogbue, tbe fair-wage officer of the government, has reported on tbe wages paid to these men. In an issue of tbe Labour Gazette of September, there is a statement of tbe qualifications of Mr. O'Donoghue for a position to which be was appointed, and tbe writer proceeds as follows :
In connection. with the duties of his office, Mr. O'Donoghue is required to report to the government on the rate of wages current in the districts where government work, whether by contract or otherwise, is being carried out. It is also his duty to assist in the preparation of * fair wages ' schedules, to be incorporated in the conditions of contracts awarded by the government, and to see that contractors comply with these conditions when made. Mr. O'Donoghue entered upon the duties of his office almost immediately after his appointment, and has since visited industrial centres in all parts of the Dominion where government work is being carried on. In one or two instances he has reported that the rates being paid were not those current in the district, and the government has taken immediate steps to secure the payment of a fair wage.
Putting aside for a moment the question of the duty of tbe government to have incorporated tbe fair-wages clause in tbe contract for this work, it would seem that the duties of Mr O'Donogbue involve his reporting to the government on tbe rate of wages paid on this government contract. On that point, we ought to have some information from tbe acting Minister of Labour. I did not quite catch from the remarks of the hon. member for Kingston what is the rate of wages paid.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAXATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY LANDS.
speechtext: $1.20 to $1.25 per day.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAXATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY LANDS.
speechtext:
On looking over the schedules of wages, many of which are incorporated in tbe Labour Gazette for September last, I find that, with one or two exceptions, the wages amount to at least $1.25, and in many cases to very much more than that, for ordinary labourers, and that in districts not remote from Kingston.
For example, take tbe drill hall at Brock-ville, ordinary labourers received $1.25, and for skilled workmen tlie rates ran up to $3 a day. In tbe works on the St. Andrew's rapids, Manitoba, ordinary labourers were paid $1.80 a day, while tbe rates for skilled workmen ran up to $4 a day. Then, take tbe case of tbe contract for a high level pier and two bulkheads, Montreal harbour-ordinary workmen, $1.25 a day, skilled workmen, $2.75, and some as high as $3.25 a day. Then, tbe contracts for tlie superstructure for the highway bridge at Ottawa, ordinary workmen, $1.35 a day, skilled workmen all the way up to $3 a day. Then, take the contract for the drill hall, Windsor, Ont.: ordinary labourers $1.50 per day, and skilled
