workmen, $3 a day. Then, certain work to be done in connection with the Chaudiere slide, Ottawa ; in respect to tbe work to be performed in Ottawa, ordinary workmen received $1.25 a day, and skilled workmen $2.25 a day. And so on, in half a dozen other cases with which I will not trouble the House. In no case, with one or two exceptions, do I find the rate for ordinary labour to be below $1.25 a day. Now, I think it would have been proper, this resolution having been passed by the House last year- and we on this side desired that it would take the form of a statute, but it did not take that form-I see no good reason why the clause should not have been inserted in this contract; and, even if not inserted, there seems no reason why Mr. O'Donoghue should not have employed himself to see that the labourers in Kingston were paid such rates as were fixed by the government themselves. The terms of the resolution of last year, so far as I could understand them, would seem to include a case of this kind. I will read a portion of it that is applicable : That it be resolved, that all government contracts should contain such conditions as will prevent abuses, which may arise from the subletting of such contracts, and that every effort should be made to secure the payment of such wages as are generally accepted as current in each trade for competent workmen in the district where the work is carried out. If the government had insisted upon this clause being inserted in this contract and had prepared such a schedule as was prepared in other eases, there is not much doubt that the wages would have been fixed at rates that would have prevented this trouble. Judging by the press reports the strike seems to be an important one-400 men out of work. The question between the men and their employers, as I understand it, is whether $1.20 a day is enough for ordinary labour or not. The newspaper report that I have is that they demanded an advance to $1.25 per day. But the hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Britton) understands that their demand is for $1.30 a day. Mr. BRITTON. They demanded an increase of 10 cents a day on whatever the amount was. Hon. Mr. SUTHERLAND. With the permission of the House, I will say a word to the hon. member (Mr. Borden, Halifax). There will be differences of opinion, of course, but a contract such as this has not been construed as one of those to which the resolution applied. Mr. BORDEN (Halifax). Is there any difference in principle ? Hon. Mr. SUTHERLAND. There may be a considerable difference in principle. Where the government let a contract they have direct control. But where they purchase goods from individual firms, I do not see how they could well go so far as to regu-171i	late wages. However, as I say, it is a question on which there are differences of opinion. The statement of the manager is that the labourers are receiving $1.20 to $1.60, which would be considerably over the average rates that the hon. gentleman has quoted as the current rates for the different districts. He quoted wages in districts all the way from Montreal to Windsor. Mr. BORDEN (Hailfax). With the hon. gentleman's permission, I would say that the increased rates to which he refers are, according to the report which is before me, not applicable to ordinary labour, but applicable to skilled labour, for instance, drillers, $1.35 ; fitters' helpers, $1.30, and so on, through a long list which I need not quote. Hon. Mr. SUTHERLAND. I am not able to say from personal knowledge, but I have stated that no information has been sent to the department in regard to the matter, nor has any application been made by either party. My hon. friend will easily see that the Department of Labour, to be effective, must act under the statute. On the other hand, it will be always ready to offer assistance that can be accepted by the parties. The object of establishing the department is to bring about conciliation between employees and employers. I am sure that the department or its officers will not stand upon any point of etiquette, but will be only too glad if they can by offering their services bring about an arrangement between the parties. As to the contract being one that would come under the resolution, there seems to be a difference of opinion. But I doubt very much if my hon. friend would say, if it were the case of a government purchase of an article from a firm or an individual that the government could interfere with the wages paid. Mr. BORDEN (Halifax). My hon. friend, of course, will see that the argument I made did not require me to go that far. I was talking about the case of a government ordering things to be manufactured by a company that does that kind of work. I do not at present, subject to my hon. friend's correction, see that there is any difference of principle between a case of that kind and the case of a government employing a man to erect a bridge. Hon. Mr. HAGGART. Or giving a contract for the making of mail bags. Hon. Mr. SUTHERLAND. Some of the officials in the different departments have put a somewhat different construction upon it. The endeavour of the department and its officials is to carry out the spirit of the resolution. So far as I am concerned, I will endeavour to take whatever action I can to bring about conciliation between the two parties. Motion agreed to, and House went into Committee of Supply.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAXATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY LANDS.
speechtext: Why is- the additional amount required ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAXATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY LANDS.
speechtext: There are three residences which we find it necessary to provide the principals of the industrial schools, at St. Paul, near Winnipeg, Calgary and Elkhorn, 81,800 each. For the Elkhorn school we have to provide for fire protection, 8400 ; for painting a portion of the building, 8300 ; Oxford House, teacher's salary, 8200 ; Island Lake, 8300 ; Norway House, enlarging the public school building, 8600 ; to provide material for boarding school, Norway House, 8100. These were matters which had been pressed upon my attention during the early part of the year, but I had not decided to recommend them until after the main estimates had been settled. I had not as much information about them as would enable me to settle them, and parties came and pressed the matter upon my attention, and gave me further information, and amongst a large number of similar applications that were made, I decided to recommend these small amounts.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAXATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY LANDS.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman will permit me to mention a matter that I should have brought to his attention when the items respecting the Geological Survey were before the House. I have had placed in my hands a letter in which it is stated that the Minister of the Interior had granted leave of absence to one of the members of the Geological Survey to do some exploring for a Dr. Mond, of England. The complaint is, that if a privilege of that kind is granted to any one person it should be granted to others. As a matter of fact, I 'think it ought not to be granted to any person. I do not know whether there is anything in the statement, but, I think it my duty to bring it to the attention of the minister.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAXATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY LANDS.
speechtext:
I may say that one of the most serious difficulties in administering the affairs of the Geological Survey consists in maintaining a Mr. SUTHERLAND (Oxford).
dividing line between work of a commercial character and work which is done for the scientific purposes of the department by officers of the Geological Survey. We continually have applications for officers of the Geological Survey to make an examination of particular places where we have reason to believe that the reports are intended to be used for speculative purposes, or for the purpose of enhancing the value of certain properties. We have endavoured consistently to avoid that in every case where it has been possible to do so. But, in the case referred to, after a good deal of consultation with Dr. Bex, the acting director of the survey, I concluded that it was a case in which we could afford in the general interests of the country, to relax the rule. Dr. Barlow is the gentleman referred to. Dr. Mond is a wealthy Englishman, who has also some pretention to being a scientific man, being a member of the Royal Society of England. He has expended, I believe, in the neighbourhood of a million dollars in the development of the nickel industry in the vicinity of Sudbury. He made a special request to the director of the survey that Dr. Barlow, who had given special attention to the deposits of nickel, should be allowed to spend six months in working up that 'portion of country, and offered to defray all his expenses, the conditions being that the survey should have the scientific results In the form of a report from Dr. Barlow at the end of the term. I am aware that it was a departure from the ordinary rule, but after consultation with the acting director, and after receiving his strong opinion to the effect that it was advisable under the circumstances, I decided to do it, and I think in this particular case it was desirable to relax the general rule. The hon. gentleman will see that, because this industry is being developed on such a large scale, the person promoting it, desiring to secure the services of this one man whom he conceived to be a man in whom he could have absolute confidence, and the whole country being interested in the development of that industry, I agreed to a departure from the rule in that case. I do not believe in permitting the officers of the Survey to be diverted from their work, but I think in this special case I was justified in doing it.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAXATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY LANDS.
speechtext:
I would think that it would be better to permit officers to perform such services only in very special cases, and I am not sure that it is wise to per-1 mit them at all, because the hon. gentleman will see that it is bound to produce feeling among other people who are seeking to develop mineral interests in adjacent territory. They will come to the hon. gentleman and ask a similar favour. If he persists in allowing that, in a great many cases, it must interfere with the work of the department, and if he does not do so it is bound to produce feeling. I think there is another reason stronger than that, and it is

that the members of the Geological Survey should be kept free from connection with business matters of this kind. The country no doubt has sustained very great loss in the death of Dr. Dawson who, in that respect, as in all other respects, set a splendid example to the members of the Geological Survey. I am of opinion from What little experience and knowledge I have of these matters, that it is not a desirable thing that members of the Geological Survey should be employed by persons in this way at all. I do not say that the circumstances in this case were not of a special character, but I th.nk it would be a wholesome rule if it were not permitted to be done at all. I think there would be less danger in that way than in pursuing the other course, because those seeking to develop the country can procure the services of experts apart from the Geological Survey. I do not think the interests of the country will suffer much by refusing the services of officers of the Geological Survey which I think they may suffer if this practice is indulged in.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAXATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY LANDS.
speechtext: Does the hon. gentleman-(Mr. Borden, Halifax) object to the principle of lending members of the Geological Survey ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAXATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY LANDS.
speechtext: To business enterprises ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAXATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY LANDS.
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAXATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY LANDS.
speechtext: Yes, I most certainly do.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAXATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY LANDS.
speechtext: Because I would think, as far as I have been able to judge by the results. that it would be rather a good thing for this country if we could persuade some body to steal them all.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAXATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY LANDS.
speechtext: Well, I do not know about that.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAXATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY LANDS.
speechtext:
If the hon. gentleman (Mr. Oliver) made this remark as a joke, I would not think it was necessary to reply to it, but I rather think he is serious on the question.	I
wholly and entirely differ from him.	I
think the country owes a great deal to these men that it will never be able to repay, and I trust that we will be able to give a reasonable appreciation to the labours of the scientific men who have devoted themselves to the country. We have men in the Geological Survey who could earn three times the salaries if they did not desire to devote all their lives to the scientific calling-in which they are engaged.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAXATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY LANDS.
speechtext:
Outside of Dr. Dawson I have had very little connection with any of them, but I have been brought into contact with two or three of them and I think they are men of high character anti ability and in every way satisfactory.
Indians-To provide an amount to promote the education of Indians in Yukon territory, $5 -*000.
- 

f

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAXATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY LANDS.
speechtext:

Dominion Lands-Chargeable to Income-Additional sum for salaries of extra clerks at head office in connection with patents for railway land grants, $3,500.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAXATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY LANDS.
speechtext: What is the necessity for so many additional clerks ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAXATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY LANDS.
speechtext:
This is simply a vote for the purpose of paying for such copying clerks as may be required for the purpose of copying patents. I took an additional grant in the main estimates of $5,000, and we find that is not likely to be quite sufficient. We hope to get the work done during the next nine or ten months. Of course, this particular vote will be expended in accordance with the Civil Service Act. Any clerks that will be employed will have to pass the civil service examination.
Dominion Lands-Chargeable to' Capital-Further amount required for surveys, $50,000.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAXATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY LANDS.
speechtext: What is the total amount for surveys, and why is a further amount required ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAXATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY LANDS.
speechtext: In the main estimates, in which we provided for surveys, the surveyor general did not include anything for surveys in the Yukon, and the estimate which we make for the work in the Yukon is as follows : We shall have eight employees besides the labouring men, and the salaries will amount to $10,145, and living allowance to $11,400, making $21,545. In addition to that there is $25,000 for -the purpose of paying the cost of survey parties, which makes altogether $46,545. There may be some small expenses in the way of the payment of labouring men required so that we have to ask for a vote in round figures of $50,000.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAXATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY LANDS.
speechtext: Why is the amount so much increased this year over last ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAXATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY LANDS.
speechtext: The department is simply struggling to keep ahead of settlement and as the lands are exhausted that have been subdivided we have to survey all parts of the country wherever the settlers go. It would be cheaper to survey in a block, but the people go wherever the land is reported to be desirable, and it is quite impossible to keep ahead of settlement with the amount of money at our disposal.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAXATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY LANDS.
speechtext: What are these surveyors doing in the Yukon ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAXATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY LANDS.
speechtext:
These gentlemen are making surveys of the creeks on which there are mining locations. The whole difficulty which arose in connection with the administration of mining claims in the early administration of that country arose from the fact that there was no survey, and the descriptions were so indeterminate that the mining recorders were necessarily led into mistakes. Now the mining recorder despatches a party to make a survey of the creek and record it. It is impossible to administer the mining laws without that.
Mr. LaRIYIERE. Are the surveys done by contract, or by the day ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAXATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY LANDS.
speechtext:
All by the day ; we cannot get them by contract there.
Mr. LaRIYIERE. Who are the surveyors?

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAXATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY LANDS.
speechtext: There are three qualified Dominion land surveyors ; James Gibbon, P. C. T. Dumais, and C. W. McPherson.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAXATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY LANDS.
speechtext: How much do you pay them ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAXATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY LANDS.
speechtext:
We give the qualified land surveyors .$150 per month with the usual monthly allowance of $150. It is very hard to keep them there.
To build fence between Ridingstone police post and Milk River along international boundary, $6,000.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAXATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY LANDS.
speechtext:
There is a fertile strip which runs up from the boundary line almost south of Lethbridge, and for many years past the American stockmen have made a practice of allowing then-cattle to drift up this fertile strip and enter the Canadian territory, eating the grass and practically driving the Canadian ranchmen out of their field. The ranchmen have made complaints continually for the last four years. Various remedies have been suggested, but I took the ground that we were not getting sufficient revenue from that country to justify us in doing anything to protect the grazing. Most of the men who are grazing cattle there were not paying? any rent, and I said that until we got some rent out of this portion of the country, we could not afford to spend any money. I think my hon. friend the Minister of Agriculture employed some line riders to keep the American cattle out, but that was abandoned. There has been a number of leases recently taken out by ranchmen in that neighbourhood, and these leases will give us a yearly revenue of about $7,000 or $8,000. There are other applications before the department which will bring that amount up to double that amount. Lately, when I was in the west, a number of these ranchmen took the trouble to come all the way down to Winnipeg to meet me, and after discussing the situation fully I thought it would be Mr. HAGGART.
economy for us to put up these fences and prevent the American cattle from drifting in.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAXATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY LANDS.
speechtext: Don't you think the ranchmen ought to build the fences themselves ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAXATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY LANDS.
speechtext: The ranchmen undertook to supervise the construction of the fence ; the government paying for the material and labour.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAXATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY LANDS.
speechtext: Who will maintain the fence in the future ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAXATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY LANDS.
speechtext:
The ranchmen undertook to maintain the fence and see that it is maintained in order.
Amount required for engraving, lithographing and printing large maps of the Dominion, $25,000.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAXATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY LANDS.
speechtext: I think the time has come when we ought to have a good map of Canada. The various departments have issued different kinds of maps for one purpose or another. My own department has been engaged in issuing sectional maps of Dominion lands, but for a considerable number of years there has been no good map of Canada. The demands that come to the government in a great many ways for an accurate map, puts us in the position of being practically compelled to do this. The geographer of the Department of the Interior, who is a very capable man, has been engaged now for over a year upon this work. The map I think will be creditable to the country. It will be engraved on copper and the details will be brought out in a thoroughly satisfactory way. Of course the preparation of a map is a very difficult task and sometimes maps are very disappointing when they are issued, but I have very great hope that this map will be a very creditable production. For the first time in Canada a map is being issued of the whole country, engraved on copper, and giving detailed information in such a way that the small places can be found without difficulty. Information regarding water powers will also be shown. We cannot hope to show them all of course, but they will be given in the more important places and the number of feet of the fall will be indicated. All valuable information which will not encumber the map too much will be included. We intend to issue a second edition giving geological information, showing the different formations, and that, I think, will be of very great interest. I expect that $25,000 will pay the expense, but it may be necessary to ask for a small supplementary vote next year.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAXATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY LANDS.
speechtext:
We have been promised the geological map for four or five years, and it is high time it should be ready. Portions of that map were engraved on copper and the government should possess the copper plates, as you need only to supplement them to a small extent for the

purpose of getting an excellent map of the Dominion. That geological map has been dribbling along for thirty years, and surely it should be ready now. I think there were large sums of money paid to the party who had the printing of the notes for the government. I would like to know if the government have possession of the plates, and intend to utilize them ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAXATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY LANDS.
speechtext: I have no doubt we have the plates, but I cannot say when we are likely to get out the ,map. Some little time ago I had a talk with Dr. Bell about it. He admitted that it was pretty far behind, and he asked me for a vote of $4,000 for the purpose of bringing it up-to-date. I am quite willing to engage that before next year I will see that every possible expedition is used in its preparation. Of course, there is a vast amount of information which has to be placed on the general map of Canada which would not be placed on the map to which my hon. friend refers. As to the copper plates for this map, we shall have them in our possession, and they will be available for any future issue, as fresh data can be engraved upon them.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAXATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY LANDS.
speechtext:
I think that possibly the delay in the issue of the map is due to differences of opinion on the part of the officers of the department as to the geological strata of the country. One lays them down in one way, and his successor changes them. I think you ought to impress on the department the necessity of immediately getting out that map.
To provide tor expenses and salaries connected with the commission appointed to inquire into halt-breed claims in the North-west Territories, out of which payment may be made to J. A. J. McKenna as half-breed commissioner, notwithstanding anything In the Civil Service Act, $10,200.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAXATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY LANDS.

Mr. LaRIVIERE. What sittings are to be held to complete the work ?
The MINISTER OF THE INTERIOR, I have not a copy of the notice sent out; but sittings will be held at Birtle, on the west side of Lake Manitoba, at Killarney, at Regina, at Calgary, at Edmonton, and probably at one or two points further north. My hon. friend will see that we have avoided holding sittings in the old province of Manitoba.
Mr. LaRIVIERE. I understand that there are a few claims in the old province of Manitoba that have not yet been disposed of.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAXATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY LANDS.
speechtext: There may be, and if such claims are brought to the attention of the commissioner, he will have authority to hold a sitting at Winnipeg.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAXATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY LANDS.
speechtext: Will there be a sitting at Winnipegosis ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAXATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY LANDS.
speechtext:
Yes, one in that neighbourhood.
To provide for costs of litigation in re Qu'-Appelle vs. the King, $5,000.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAXATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY LANDS.
speechtext: What is that ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAXATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY LANDS.

Further amount required for the cost of investigations and demarcations in connection with the international boundary, and other astronomical work of the department, $27,500.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAXATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY LANDS.
speechtext:
I explained, when the supplementary estimates for the current year were before the House, that we were now engaged in preparing for remarking the international boundary line under an arrangement with the United States government-not a treaty-at certain points where the mounds and posts have been removed. The total estimate was $35,000. We took an estimate of $7,500 .which paid the expenses up to the 1st of July, and this is the balance.
Mr. LaRIVIERE. Would it not be possible to arrange with the United States to remark the south-eastern boundary of Manitoba, in order to avoid the crooked line that has been made there, and to obtain that little portion of territory which properly belongs to the province of Manitoba, but which is now claimed by the United States.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAXATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY LANDS.
speechtext:
I
do not think there would be the least use of

holding out any encouragement that any arrangement satisfactory to us could be made in regard to that piece of territory. There is no doubt, I think, that the United States are entitled to it under the agreement made. The only way tq get it would be to trade off something else for it. Since my term of office there has been no communication in regard to it, but there was in a former period, and no encouragement was held out by the United States that they would relinquish that piece of territory.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAXATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY LANDS.
speechtext: I would like to know what is the state of the facts in regard to the international line between Canada and the United States. I tried to ascertain by examining ' Hansard ' for 1899 and 1900, and I found that the premier mentioned that a proposal had been made to the United States. When the arrangements were completed the papers were to have been laid before, the House. I have looked over the indices of 1899 and 1900, and can not find any reference to the papers having come down.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAXATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY LANDS.
speechtext: The papers have not been brought down. In pursuance of the arrangement arrived at to agree on a provisional boundary, commissioners were appointed by the two governments. We appointed Mr. W. F. King, chief astronomer of the Department of the Interior, who had been commissioner when the former arrangement was made. He proceeded with the United States commissioner, and they marked out a provisional boundary line between British Columbia and this country. The part of the boundary line which required to be marked was that extending westward from Chilkoot Pass, covering the territory north of what is known as Pyramid Harbour. There was no necessity for marking the boundary in the Chilkoot Pass, because it was agreed that the summit should be the provisional boundary. The same may be said of the White Pass. There is no travel at other than these points because they are simply mountain ranges. But there is travel by way of Pyramid Harbour and what is known as the Dalton trail. Of course there it was necessary to make a provisional boundary. These lines the commissioners have marked. The papers were only laid before me for my formal approval a few days ago, and the order in council approving of them is only recently passed. We can have the papers laid on the Table before the House rises.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAXATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY LANDS.
speechtext:
I would be very glad if the hon. gentleman would do so. I think that the papers should he printed and put in the hands of every member.

Mr. BORDEN (Halifax. I was not objecting, but only wanted to know why there was a special vote.

ago Dr. Rand's dictionary was undertaken by the Dominion government, and a portion of the work remained undone, and it was deemed well to take an appropriation of $1,000 a year ago. We have only spent a very small sum, and this is a revote.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAXATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY LANDS.
speechtext: As we are discussing estimates of the Interior Department, I would ask the bon. minister if the geological branch is confined altogether to minerals ? maintopic: SUPPLY-TAXATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY LANDS.
speechtext: I may explain this case generally, though the Solicitor General will give further information if it is desired. This is to pay the legal expenses for prosecuting a suit against a company in Ottawa with which the government had difficulty.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAXATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY LANDS.
speechtext: What was the difficulty?

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAXATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY LANDS.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAXATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY LANDS.
speechtext: If the government have practically obtained a decision, why is it that the expenses should be so high as to require this amount of money ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAXATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY LANDS.
speechtext: If there is any question I would be contented to leave the matter for the Solicitor General to explain. I am not quite prepared to say at this moment that the matter has been finally decided.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAXATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY LANDS.
speechtext:
This may be to provide for expenses which may be recovered. The hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Fielding) might make a note of it and explain, the matter more fully at a later sitting. In the meantime, let the item pass.
Miscellaneous-To provide for expenses of reception to their Royal Highnesses the Duke and Duchess of Cornwall and York, $120,000.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAXATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY LANDS.
speechtext:
This item does not require much explanation. We are all aware that, to the satisfaction of the people of the whole Dominion, Her late Majesty was pleased to express her willingness that their Royal Highnesses the Duke and Duchess of Cornwall and York should
pay a visit to Canada. The death of the Sovereign created some doubt as to whether this would be carried out; but, the King has been pleased to confirm the decision given by the late Sovereign. As it is well known, their Royal Highnesses are now in Australia. It is expected that they will reach Canada in the autumn. The time allowed for their visit is but too short. According to the plans prepared by the Imperial government, they will be here but thirty-two days. , Up to the present time, we have no detailed plan of arrangements for the visit to the Dominion. No doubt, later on, the official programme will be prepared. We shall be subject to such arrangements as will be agreeable to the Imperial authorities. Our idea is that in most of the provinces the local governments and municipal authorities will make liberal provision for the reception of the royal party. But, here and there there will be links to fill in. The royal party will cross the continent and will return. It was thought they might be induced to land on the Pacific coast and cross to the Atlantic. However, for various reasons, that was found inconvenient. They will land on the Atlantic coast, there is still some question whether at Halifax or at Quebec. This will be decided soon. The present vote, as I have said, is to make provision for the proper reception of their Royal Highnesses, and to supply deficiencies in the provisions made by municipal or provincial governments. Of course, we are all anxious that the reception of the royal pair should be characterized by the dignity which is due to their distinguished position. Therefore, we think it well to take this general vote. -

I desire to bring to the attention of the acting Postmaster General a matter which I brought to the attention of the Postmaster General in 1899 and 1900. This is a grievance with respect to private mail bags, the gentleman complaining being Mr. W. C. Henley, of Spry Bay, Halifax county. The Postmaster General complied with the request that I mad^ in 1899, and restored to this man the privilege of having his mail brought to him in a private mail bag; a practice that prevails in many other places in the province and in the Dominion. Afterwards, some technical objection was raised with regard to it. I have pointed out that the same practice prevails regarding two or three other persons in the county of Halifax. This same objection prevails with regard to these. I find that the privilege which Mr. Henley asks for is allowed to Henry Hall, John Kirker, Alice McKenzie and John G. Reynolds, very respectable people in the county. It is not a question of cost at all. The post office carrier is willing to bring the bag back. Mr. Henley is perfectly willing to say to the Post Office Department that he does not require them to be responsible for the mails so delivered. An objection has been raised on a ground which the hon. gentleman will see, if he looks at the correspondence, applies to at least three other cases in the county. I say that all those men should be treated exactly alike. If it is not right in Mr. Henley's case, it is not right in any case ; but if it is right in other eases, he should be allowed the same privilege.

speechtext: I see there is no provision made for a general increase in the letter carriers' salaries. The acting Postmaster General and the Minister of Finance will remember that a day or two previous to the Postmaster General leaving for Australia, he promised a delegation that he was leaving a memorandum for the consideration of the government favourable to the request that was then being made. maintopic: SUPPLY-TAXATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY LANDS.
speechtext: I may say to my hon. friend that the Postmaster General, as he knows, left rather hurriedly, and this is one of the few matters that he left for consideration. He had two or three plans under consideration, and with regard to them there was a difference of opinion. I came to the conclusion that it was in the interest of the letter carriers that this matter should be left over until the next session. I am satisfied, after the consideration that I have been able to give it, and after a consultation with a deputation of letter carriers and with my colleagues, that it would be to their advantage to have this matter left over until next session, when a plan that I think is sure to meet with their wishes, will be carried out.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAXATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY LANDS.
speechtext: The case of the letter carriers is apt to suffer somewhat by delay. It will be remembered that their case is principally based upon the ground that the cost of living has materially increased in this country during the last two or three years.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAXATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY LANDS.
speechtext:
I think it is discreditable to the government that no conclusion has been arrived at in this case. We know that the government has not given the statutory increases to which the letter carriers are entitled. We know that the government has not considered, favourably at any rate, the question of increasing the pay of the letter carriers. Memorials have been presented and facts have been given for the increase of their salaries, and I think they have made a strong case. We were led to believe that this matter was going to be provided for by the Postmaster General, and now we have the acknowledgment of the acting Postmaster General that nothing has been done in the matter. Of course, the acting minister may feel that it is not incumbent on him to take any part in the matter. I think it is, because the absence of a minister is no reason why the public service should suffer, and why injustice should be done to a large army of employees who do their duty faithfully and efficiently, and who are perhaps

the most hard-worked officers in the whole public service. We had an assurance from the Postmaster General last year that during the recess, the matter would be investigated and justice done to the letter carriers. But so far he has not redeemed his promise.
I think the statement made by the acting Postmaster General that the scheme will be more satisfactory if left over until next year, is less satisfactory still, because that was the story told last year. The letter carriers are losing their statutory increases, to which they are entitled, and they are losing the larger consideration of a general increase in salaries, making the maximum higher than it is at present. I think they are at present the most underpaid of all the civil service officials.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAXATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY LANDS.
speechtext: There are two sides to that question. I agree with the hon. gentleman that we have no right to shirk the question on account of the absence of the Postmaster General. But there is a difference of opinion with regard to the best way to meet their wishes. My hon. friend must not forget that he was a member of the late government, which passed an Act by whieh the salaries were reduced and fixed.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAXATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY LANDS.
speechtext: Did the minister say the salaries were reduced ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAXATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY LANDS.
speechtext: I understood so, speaking subject to correction.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAXATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY LANDS.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAXATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY LANDS.
speechtext: I would ask my hon. friend to look into the facts.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAXATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY LANDS.
speechtext: ^1 have done so.

And we will decide as to whether it was not under the Act of the late government. There are a great many cases that have come under my notice, and I have done all I could under the regulations to better the condition of carriers in the cities, and I think to the satisfaction of those directly interested. X am satisfied it will be in the interest of the letter carriers. It is only a matter of a few months when we will have an opportunity of agreeing upon a plan that will be in their interests.

speechtext: I would like to call the attention of the kon. acting Postmaster General to the fact that the mails which arrive at Summerside in Prince Edward Island every evening from Pointe du Chene are transferred to Charlottetown, are there assorted after going over fifty miles one way and are then sent back over the same route to the people living in the western part of Prince county to be distributed twenty-four hours after they arrive at Summerside. maintopic: SUPPLY-TAXATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY LANDS.

speechtext: I may say that the main estimates are prepared at an early period, and we make provision for what we think will do ; but on coming nearer to the beginnig of the year, we find that calls are made upon us which the main esti-. mates do not cover. SUPPLY-TAXATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY LANDS.
speechtext: I cannot do that.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAXATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY LANDS.
speechtext:
He still leaves himself *open to come next year and ask as much as he likes.
To pay H. A. Nelson & Son interest at 5 per cent on $1,395.25 from May, 1892, to July 1, 1901, $633.67.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAXATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY LANDS.
speechtext: Why is there a special vote for this interest apart from the vote for the amount of the capital ? Is this an afterthought ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAXATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY LANDS.
speechtext: No, it was omitted by error in the supplementaries. My hon. colleague, the Finance Minister, suggested at the time that I should let the item drop and put both capital and interest in the additional supplementaries, but I thought it better to let it go through as it was and then bring in an additional vote for the interest.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAXATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY LANDS.
speechtext: Was the Department of Justice consulted ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAXATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY LANDS.
speechtext: No, it is jmrely a question of equity and not of law. The firm had imported the goods and paid the duty on them. A part were removed and a part were not removed. A fire took place in the warehouse which destroyed the part not removed, and we are refunding duty on that part.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAXATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY LANDS.
speechtext: The government is not liable for the safety of goods imported into the country. In this case the duty had been paid and the goods were released.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAXATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY LANDS.
speechtext: No doubt legally they had no claim. But the fire took place the very day the duty was paid, and before the parties had time to remove all of them. Other goods had to be import-ted in their place, on which the duty was paid.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAXATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY LANDS.
speechtext: It does not alter the case whether the goods were one day in the government warehouse or ten days, and whenever goods are destroyed by fire other goods must be imported to replace them. I do not see any reason in equity why a different course should be taken in the case of Nelson Bros, than that of any other person who loses goods by fire on which the duty is paid.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAXATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY LANDS.
speechtext:
The question of the insurable interest in these goods influences very much in all cases of the kind. In ordinary cases the goods are removed from the ship and placed in the man's own warehouse, where he can protect them by insurance. These were practically in transit between the ship and Nelson Bros', store, and before they could get into the store they were destroyed by fire. They were no doubt insured while on board the vessel, but that insurance ceased as soon as they left the vessel, and before Nelson Bros, had time

to reinsure them in their own warehouse they were destroyed by fire in the government warehouse. When these goods were landed they would not have been covered by a marine insurance policy. Messrs. Nelson have represented-and they are a reputable firm-that they would have had them insured if they had the time to get them into their warehouse. They were destroyed the same night while stored in the government warehouse.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAXATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY LANDS.
speechtext: Not a government warehouse-the government does not take into customs warehouse more than one package in ten or fifteen.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAXATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY LANDS.
speechtext: I do not mean that they were in a bonded warehouse.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAXATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY LANDS.
speechtext: The minister means simply that the government has a covered shed in which the goods of the people are put to protect them from the elements. It cannot be said that they were in the custody of the government at all. As soon as the duties are" paid, the goods are relieved and can be taken away. The duty having been paid, I think it was not an act of equity that the money should be refunded to H. A. Nelson & Son, nor the interest either.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAXATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY LANDS.
speechtext: Were there other claims made for goods destroyed at the time, or were there no other goods destroyed than "those of H. A. Nelson & Son ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAXATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY LANDS.
speechtext: A great many goods were consumed, but these were the only goods upon which the duties had been paid. If they had not paid the duty, they would not have been obliged to pay the duty at all, the goods having been destroyed. Or, had the goods been in their own warehouse, they would have been insured. The government loses nothing, because, as I said, there had to be a re-importation of these goods. As to the point that the hon. member for West York (Mr. Wallace) mentions, as to asking the Department of Justice whether the government were legally liable, I think that the difficulty of the previous government in allowing the claim was not that the law was against it, but they did not take the course we are taking in asking parliament to vote the money. I think it was not hostility to the claim that prevented it being allowed, but it was one of those cases where a claim was not settled, and goes on from year to year.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAXATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY LANDS.
speechtext: No, I remember that there was a thorough investigation.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAXATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY LANDS.
speechtext: I do not think the record shows that. I think the record will show that the hon. gentleman favoured the payment.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAXATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY LANDS.
speechtext:
It was before I became Controller. But, in our time this claim was thoroughly investigated, and it was found that there was no legal claim, and that
there was no difference between having paid the duty and not having paid it. As to their having them insured if they had got them into their own warehouse, we do not know that.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAXATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY LANDS.
speechtext: That is the usual custom.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAXATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY LANDS.
speechtext: Usually a man has his stock insured for a certain sum.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAXATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY LANDS.
speechtext: Then, these would have been covered, a general policy of insurance would have covered them.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAXATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY LANDS.
speechtext:
But one is not allowed to insure for a hundred cents on the dollar, but for only two-thirds of the value ; therefore, the duty would not have been insured in that case.
